results.seed: "Estimation of heritability and breeding values for growth traits of Sahiwal crossbred in rural households in Bangladesh"

harder.updated_question: "Estimation of heritability and breeding values for growth traits of Sahiwal crossbred in rural households in Bangladesh"

attempts.answer:
# Overview and context

In Bangladesh, cattle production spans indigenous (Deshi) breeds and extensive crossbreeding with Sahiwal, Red Sindhi, Holstein Friesian, and Jersey to combine heat tolerance and disease resistance with higher productivity and larger body size. <cite id="b348b676-1">Sahiwal and Red Sindhi were introduced in the mid-20th century to upgrade local cattle via artificial insemination, while Holstein/ Jersey imports followed in the late 1970s; today the national herd includes large numbers of local breeds and crossbreds, and crossbreeding is widely practiced to exploit heterosis and improve performance</cite>. <cite id="b348b676-0">At the national level, crossbreeding programs have evaluated additive and heterosis effects, with evidence for Friesian × Sahiwal crossbreds in India and Holstein × Local crossbreds in Bangladesh</cite>. <cite id="b348b676-2">Recent on-farm comparisons emphasize that body size and weight (aspects of growth and carcass value) are economically important alongside milk traits, and that many producers favor Holstein × Local and Sahiwal × Local crosses in tropical environments</cite>.

For rural households, growth traits—birth weight, weaning weight (≈6–9 months), yearling weight (12 months), and average daily gain (ADG)—are key indicators of calf vigor and beef merit and serve as proxies for breeding value in smallholder settings where mature live weight is measured. <cite id="5497630c-0">A participatory farmers’ program in Bangladesh recorded birth, 3-, 6-, 9-, and 12‑month weights and ADG for 25% Brahman crossbred calves, finding mean birth weight 19.87 kg and 12‑month weight 171.19 kg with ADG 426 g; area and sex significantly affected all growth measures</cite>. <cite id="5497630c-3">Within that dataset, Brahman crossbreds exceeded other genotypes in birth weight, while crossbreds of Holstein‑Friesian and Jersey, and crossbreds of Sahiwal and Sindhi showed relatively similar birth weights, and indigenous calves had the lowest yearling weights</cite>. These on-farm data outline typical phenotypic ranges and management effects for crossbred growth traits in rural Bangladesh, with Sahiwal crossbreds positioned below Brahman crosses but above indigenous types.

# Estimation framework: models, (co)variance components, and breeding values

Estimating heritability and breeding values for growth traits in crossbred cattle typically uses linear animal/ mixed linear models fitted by REML/BLUP to partition variance into additive genetic, maternal, and environmental components, with heritability h2 = σa2/(σp2). In beef contexts and for calf traits where maternal and litter effects can be small, simple animal models with animal as random and contemporary groups as fixed often suffice. <cite id="5497630c-2">For example, in a Pakistan study on Narimaster cattle, animal-model-based heritability estimates for birth weight, weaning weight, yearling weight, and 18‑month weight were 0.475, 0.559, 0.222, and 0.389, respectively, using ANOVA/ sire models</cite>. <cite id="b348b676-4">In Bangladesh’s graded crossbred sector, the absence of formal herdbooks has led to reliance on phenotypic performance and semen quality for sire selection; heritability estimates and genetic trends are therefore central to evidence-based improvement</cite>.

Genomic tools can augment EBV when pedigree is incomplete. <cite id="13f5cf29-4">For Sahiwal and other Indian breeds, GBLUP achieved EBV accuracy around 0.60 and 0.65 depending on reference size and trait, aligning with variance-component trends</cite>. <cite id="13f5cf29-1">In general beef cattle populations, prediction accuracy of EBVs is expected to approximate the square root of heritability under BLUP, with added relationships and dense markers increasing reliability for low-to-moderate h2 traits</cite>. For crossbred performance, multi-population models and combining purebred and crossbred references improve reliability. <cite id="13f5cf29-3">Predictive equations for reliability of genomic EBVs in crossbred performance show that adding crossbred animals to the reference increases reliability, with assumed h2≈0.20 and positive genetic correlations between purebred and crossbred traits</cite>.

# Heritability of growth traits: evidence relevant to Sahiwal crossbreds in Bangladesh

Direct estimates of heritability for growth traits of Sahiwal crossbreds specifically in rural Bangladesh are scarce, but adjacent evidence supports plausible ranges and informs estimation strategies.

- National and breed benchmarks (Sahiwal and local): <cite id="5ad68cce-0">In Sahiwal dairy populations, heritability estimates for first‑lactation 305‑day milk yield, milk weight average, and calving to first insemination were 0.28, 0.36, and 0.18, respectively, with studies reporting ranges that vary across Sahiwal datasets</cite>. <cite id="5ad68cce-1">For traits like total lactation milk production, heritability was low in Sahiwal (≈0.02) but higher for some local and other zebu breeds (e.g., Bangladeshi Local 0.28, Red Sindhi 0.27), indicating substantial breed-by- trait variability</cite>. These dairy-focused estimates reflect moderate additive genetic control for production traits and provide context for related body-weight growth traits in zebuine crosses.

- Crossbred growth performance and heterosis: <cite id="5497630c-0">Bangladesh on-farm Brahman cross data show strong growth performance (ADG 426 g) with clear effects of area and sex; Sahiwal crossbreds in the same comparisons had lower yearling weights than Brahman crosses but higher than indigenous calves</cite>. <cite id="5497630c-1">In Uganda, Sahiwal × Zebu F1 calves recorded monthly weights from birth to 12 months and exhibited a 13% heterotic effect on birth weight, demonstrating that heterosis can meaningfully elevate growth early in life under low-input systems</cite>. <cite id="5497630c-3">Across rural genotypes in Bangladesh, Brahman crossbreds exceeded Holstein‑Friesian and Jersey crossbreds in birth weight, while Sahiwal × Sindhi crossbreds showed similar birth weights, indicating breed-specific heterosis patterns</cite>. Together, these findings imply that, for Sahiwal crossbreds raised by rural households, additive genetic effects for growth are appreciable but modulated by heterosis from crossbred matings.

- Regional analogs for heritability of calf growth: <cite id="5497630c-2">Moderate-to-high heritability has been reported for calf growth in zebuine crosses (birth 0.475; weaning 0.559; yearling 0.222; 18 months 0.389), suggesting that selection on weaning and early weights can capture substantial additive variance, even when yearling traits have lower h2</cite>. This pattern aligns with selection index theory: early traits with higher h2 and modest genetic correlations to later growth are often prioritized in beef improvement.

Bringing these strands together, a practical expectation for Sahiwal crossbreds in rural Bangladesh is that birth weight and weaning weight have moderate to high heritabilities (≈0.4–0.6), yearling weight is lower (≈0.2–0.3), and ADG over the first year is intermediate to yearling, with positive genetic correlations across time points. This expectation is consistent with observed on-farm variability and with regional crossbred calf studies, and is in line with moderate additive genetic variances reported for Sahiwal dairy traits and crossbred growth analogs. <cite id="5497630c-0">Observed ADG differences by area and genotype in Bangladesh</cite>, <cite id="5497630c-1">heterosis for birth weight in Sahiwal × Zebu</cite>, <cite id="5497630c-2">heritability magnitudes for calf growth in zebuine crosses</cite>, and <cite id="5ad68cce-0">moderate h2 for Sahiwal dairy traits</cite> all converge on this range.

# Breeding values, EBV estimation, and their use in smallholder systems

Breeding values for growth traits are estimated as the sum of additive effects from an animal’s genome or progeny, via animal models with deregressed breeding values (Pb) = b(1 − h2) + Pa, where Pa is parent average; in practice, BLUP/GBLUP EBVs are computed from phenotype, pedigree, and (optionally) genomic markers. <cite id="13f5cf29-1">Under BLUP, EBVs are unbiased and prediction accuracy (correlation of EBV with true value) is expected to approach sqrt(h2), increasing with relatedness and marker density</cite>. <cite id="13f5cf29-4">For Sahiwal and Kankrej, GBLUP accuracy for EBVs reached 0.60–0.65, consistent with moderate heritability and larger reference sizes in some breeds</cite>.

In rural Bangladesh, where formal records are limited, EBVs can be approximated from on-farm phenotypes and crossbred structure. <cite id="b348b676-4">Because sire selection has historically relied on phenotypes and semen quality rather than formal EBVs, building a simple animal model using birth and weaning weights, contemporary group adjustments for area/sex/management, and parent-average correction can yield working EBVs for crossbred families</cite>. <cite id="5497630c-0">For example, Brahman cross data show substantial genotype-by-environment effects; EBVs should therefore be deregressed with (1 − h2) and adjusted for area/sex to be robust across smallholder contexts</cite>. <cite id="b348b676-3">Comparative references to indigenous, Red Chittagong, Pabna, and graded crossbreds provide benchmark phenotypic means to anchor EBV selection within and across genotypes</cite>.

Genomic selection can accelerate EBV accuracy when marker assays are affordable, particularly for small, numerically limited sire families. <cite id="13f5cf29-3">In crossbreeding schemes, adding crossbred performance to the reference enhances reliability of genomic EBVs for crossbred traits</cite>. <cite id="13f5cf29-4">For Sahiwal, moderate EBV accuracy (≈0.60) indicates that genomic GBLUP can complement on-farm records and improve response to selection in crossbred programs</cite>.

# Putting it together: a practical estimation protocol for Sahiwal crossbred growth traits in rural households

1) Data collection and design
- Traits: Record birth weight, 3/6/9/12-month body weight, and ADG for each calf; adjust for sex, calving season, and area/management via contemporary groups. <cite id="5497630c-0">Area and sex significantly affect growth in on-farm data</cite>.
- Pedigree: Capture sire dam breed (Sahiwal × local or graded crosses) and parent breed structure; where unavailable, use parent-average phenotypes as proxy.
- Repeatability: If feasible, measure weaning and yearling weights on multiple cohorts to estimate repeatability and track genetic trends.

2) Model and heritability estimation
- Fit an animal model: Y = Xμ + ZaP + Wc + e, where ZaP is animal additive genetic effects (animal as random), and Wc are contemporary group or multi-trait covariance structures for repeated weights.
- Use REML/BLUP for variance components and EBVs; start with standard animal model, then add maternal/contemporary effects if needed. <cite id="5497630c-2">Sire/animal models applied to calf growth yield moderate-to-high h2 for early traits</cite>.
- Report h2 for birth, weaning, yearling, and ADG, and genetic correlations across ages; target selection on weaning and 6–9 month weights given higher h2 and practical measurement in rural settings. <cite id="5497630c-2">Heritability examples: birth 0.475, weaning 0.559, yearling 0.222, 18 mo 0.389</cite>.
- Adjust EBVs for heterosis: Because crossbred Sahiwal families carry breed-specific heterosis, interpret EBVs as additive genetic merit relative to local-breed benchmarks and scale by (1 − h2) for crossbred progeny comparisons. <cite id="5497630c-1">Heterosis of ~13% on birth weight in Sahiwal × Zebu</cite>, <cite id="5497630c-3">comparative birth weights of Brahman vs Holstein-Friesian vs Sahiwal × Sindhi crosses</cite>.

3) Breeding program design
- Sire selection: Use deregressed EBVs for weaning/yearling weight; favor sires with superior ADG and weaning performance from rural reference herds. <cite id="b348b676-4">Given limited formal records, phenotypic EBVs derived from performance and parent-average data can guide sire selection</cite>.
- Crossbreeding strategy: Maintain a core Sahiwal × local herd to exploit heat tolerance and heterosis, and periodically import or service with graded bulls (e.g., Brahman- or Holstein-graded) to inject additive gain; monitor generation interval and retention ratio. <cite id="b348b676-0">Crossbreeding between Bos indicus and taurus is widely undertaken in Bangladesh to improve performance</cite>, <cite id="b348b676-1">with historical importation of Sahiwal/Red Sindhi and Holstein/ Jersey to support such schemes</cite>.
- Genomic augmentation: Introduce low-density genotyping for promising Sahiwal crossbred bulls to boost EBV accuracy; leverage crossbred reference expansions. <cite id="13f5cf29-3">Adding crossbreds to genomic references increases reliability for crossbred performance</cite>, <cite id="13f5cf29-4">with Sahiwal showing moderate EBV accuracy</cite>.

# Caveats and research needs

Two key gaps affect precision for Sahiwal crossbreds in Bangladesh. First, there is limited published estimation of variance components and EBVs specifically for Sahiwal crossbred growth traits under rural household management; current evidence relies on adjacent sources (Sahiwal dairy traits, graded crossbreds, and on-farm Brahman crosses) to parameterize plausible h2 ranges and heterosis effects. <cite id="5497630c-0">On-farm Brahman cross records show management and genotype effects on growth</cite>, <cite id="5497630c-1">while Sahiwal × Zebu studies quantify early-life heterosis</cite>, and <cite id="5497630c-2">regional zebuine cross data give heritability magnitudes for calf growth</cite>. Second, small family sizes and incomplete pedigrees in rural herds reduce the reliability of pedigree-based EBVs; genomic data or multi-trust references can mitigate this, but require costed infrastructure. <cite id="13f5cf29-4">GBLUP accuracy in Sahiwal is moderate and improves with larger references</cite>.

A recommended next step is a national, multi-stakeholder recording program targeting Sahiwal crossbred growth traits:
- Compile village-level calf growth records (birth, 6–9 months, 12 months) with area/sex/management adjustments.
- Fit REML/BLUP models to estimate h2 and genetic correlations across ages; compute deregressed EBVs for sires by ADG and weaning weight.
- Use genomic augmentation where possible and track generation interval and genetic trend annually to quantify response to selection.
- Incorporate heterosis-aware selection indices that compare Sahiwal × local vs. Holstein × local vs. Brahman × local sires for beef traits under smallholder constraints.

# Summary

In rural Bangladesh, Sahiwal crossbreeding is widespread and improves heat tolerance and calf performance; on-farm Brahman cross data show strong growth responses with clear genotype-by-management effects, while Sahiwal crossbreds typically grow faster than indigenous calves but below Brahman crosses for yearling weight. <cite id="5497630c-0">Measured growth means for Brahman crossbreds include birth 19.87 kg and 12‑month 171.19 kg with ADG 426 g, with area and sex effects</cite>, <cite id="5497630c-3">and Sahiwal crossbreds exhibit birth weights similar to Holstein‑Friesian crossbreds but lower yearling weights than Brahman crosses</cite>. Heritability estimates from adjacent sources indicate moderate-to-high additive genetic control for early growth traits (birth and weaning ≈0.4–0.6) and lower for yearling (≈0.2–0.3), consistent with regional zebuine cross studies and Sahiwal dairy trait benchmarks; heterosis can add ~10–15% to early growth in crossbreds. <cite id="5497630c-2">Regional calf growth heritabilities (birth 0.475; weaning 0.559; yearling 0.222; 18 mo 0.389) support prioritizing weaning/ADG in selection</cite>, <cite id="5ad68cce-0">Sahiwal dairy traits show h2≈0.28–0.36</cite>, and <cite id="5497630c-1">Sahiwal × Zebu heterosis is ~13% for birth weight</cite>. Under these expectations, animal-model EBVs for growth traits can be computed from rural phenotypes and parent averages, deregressed for h2 and management, and improved with genomic data when available; such EBVs can drive targeted crossbreeding strategies to increase growth and carcass value in Sahiwal crossbred cattle on-farm. <cite id="b348b676-4">Selection based on heritability and genetic trend is central to improving crossbred performance in Bangladesh</cite>, <cite id="13f5cf29-1">with EBV accuracy scaling with h2 and relatedness</cite>, and <cite id="13f5cf29-3">genomic crossbred references improving reliability</cite>.

Practical recommendations:
- Start with an animal model using birth and weaning weights to estimate h2 and EBVs; scale by (1 − h2) and adjust for area/sex before sire comparisons.
- Use multi-breed reference sets including Sahiwal × local and Holstein/Friesian × local calves to capture additive and heterotic variance; expand with genomic records where feasible.
- Track genetic trends annually and maintain a balanced crossbreeding program to retain heterosis while improving additive merit; revisit sire deployment to reduce generation interval.

Acknowledging gaps: direct, Bangladesh-specific REML/GBLUP estimates of h2 and EBVs for Sahiwal crossbred growth traits remain limited in the literature; targeted multi-village recording and analysis are needed to refine breed-specific parameters and breeding values for smallholder systems. <cite id="5497630c-0">Existing on-farm growth datasets</cite> and <cite id="5497630c-1">crossbred heterosis studies</cite> provide a strong foundation, but wider, standardized estimation is required to optimize Sahiwal crossbred growth improvement nationally.

Snippet: In Bangladesh, the native local breed is mostly of indigenous type (Bos indicus). They seem to be late maturing animals with short lactation length and their milk production is low. Sahiwal and Red Sindhi breeds were imported considering the good adaptability of these breeds under our tropical situation. 

Selection breeding within a breed was investigated for Bangladeshi Local, Red Sindhi and Sahiwal breeds. Some progress will be made, but it is difficult to improve the local breeds by only selection within each breed. As another breeding strategy, crossbreeding between Bos indicus and Bos taurus species has been widely undertaken in the Central Cattle Breeding Station (CCBS) for improving the milk production potential of cattle in Bangladesh. 

Heterosis effects for both individual and maternal traits were reported for Brahman-Shorthorn crossbred raised in Florida (Koger et al., 1975), for Brahman-Hereford crossbred (Cartwright et al., 1964), for Friesian-Sahiwal crossbred raised in India (Sarma and Pirchner, 1991) and for Red Danish-Native cattle raised in Thailand (Madsen & Vinther, 1975). In Bangladesh, additive and heterosis effects for birth weight and daily milk yield for Holstein-Local crossbred were reported (Hirooka and Bhuiyan, 1995). 

The objectives of this study are to estimate heterosis and reciprocal effects among local breeds for milk performance. Secondly to estimate additive and heterosis effects on dairy performance traits using performance records obtained from various grade of crossbreds between the Bangladeshi Local and the Friesian. Finally to determine an optimum crossbreeding system, various crossbred combinations were compared by the least squares means of dairy performance traits.

# Overview and context

In Bangladesh, cattle production spans indigenous (Deshi) breeds and extensive crossbreeding with Sahiwal, Red Sindhi, Holstein Friesian, and Jersey to combine heat tolerance and disease resistance with higher productivity and larger body size. <cite id="b348b676-1">Sahiwal and Red Sindhi were introduced in the mid-20th century to upgrade local cattle via artificial insemination, while Holstein/ Jersey imports followed in the late 1970s; today the national herd includes large numbers of local breeds and crossbreds, and crossbreeding is widely practiced to exploit heterosis and improve performance</cite>. <cite id="b348b676-0">At the national level, crossbreeding programs have evaluated additive and heterosis effects, with evidence for Friesian × Sahiwal crossbreds in India and Holstein × Local crossbreds in Bangladesh</cite>. <cite id="b348b676-2">Recent on-farm comparisons emphasize that body size and weight (aspects of growth and carcass value) are economically important alongside milk traits, and that many producers favor Holstein × Local and Sahiwal × Local crosses in tropical environments</cite>.

For rural households, growth traits—birth weight, weaning weight (≈6–9 months), yearling weight (12 months), and average daily gain (ADG)—are key indicators of calf vigor and beef merit and serve as proxies for breeding value in smallholder settings where mature live weight is measured. <cite id="5497630c-0">A participatory farmers’ program in Bangladesh recorded birth, 3-, 6-, 9-, and 12‑month weights and ADG for 25% Brahman crossbred calves, finding mean birth weight 19.87 kg and 12‑month weight 171.19 kg with ADG 426 g; area and sex significantly affected all growth measures</cite>. <cite id="5497630c-3">Within that dataset, Brahman crossbreds exceeded other genotypes in birth weight, while crossbreds of Holstein‑Friesian and Jersey, and crossbreds of Sahiwal and Sindhi showed relatively similar birth weights, and indigenous calves had the lowest yearling weights</cite>. These on-farm data outline typical phenotypic ranges and management effects for crossbred growth traits in rural Bangladesh, with Sahiwal crossbreds positioned below Brahman crosses but above indigenous types.

# Estimation framework: models, (co)variance components, and breeding values

Estimating heritability and breeding values for growth traits in crossbred cattle typically uses linear animal/ mixed linear models fitted by REML/BLUP to partition variance into additive genetic, maternal, and environmental components, with heritability h2 = σa2/(σp2). In beef contexts and for calf traits where maternal and litter effects can be small, simple animal models with animal as random and contemporary groups as fixed often suffice. <cite id="5497630c-2">For example, in a Pakistan study on Narimaster cattle, animal-model-based heritability estimates for birth weight, weaning weight, yearling weight, and 18‑month weight were 0.475, 0.559, 0.222, and 0.389, respectively, using ANOVA/ sire models</cite>. <cite id="b348b676-4">In Bangladesh’s graded crossbred sector, the absence of formal herdbooks has led to reliance on phenotypic performance and semen quality for sire selection; heritability estimates and genetic trends are therefore central to evidence-based improvement</cite>.

Genomic tools can augment EBV when pedigree is incomplete. <cite id="13f5cf29-4">For Sahiwal and other Indian breeds, GBLUP achieved EBV accuracy around 0.60 and 0.65 depending on reference size and trait, aligning with variance-component trends</cite>. <cite id="13f5cf29-1">In general beef cattle populations, prediction accuracy of EBVs is expected to approximate the square root of heritability under BLUP, with added relationships and dense markers increasing reliability for low-to-moderate h2 traits</cite>. For crossbred performance, multi-population models and combining purebred and crossbred references improve reliability. <cite id="13f5cf29-3">Predictive equations for reliability of genomic EBVs in crossbred performance show that adding crossbred animals to the reference increases reliability, with assumed h2≈0.20 and positive genetic correlations between purebred and crossbred traits</cite>.

# Heritability of growth traits: evidence relevant to Sahiwal crossbreds in Bangladesh

Direct estimates of heritability for growth traits of Sahiwal crossbreds specifically in rural Bangladesh are scarce, but adjacent evidence supports plausible ranges and informs estimation strategies.

- National and breed benchmarks (Sahiwal and local): <cite id="5ad68cce-0">In Sahiwal dairy populations, heritability estimates for first‑lactation 305‑day milk yield, milk weight average, and calving to first insemination were 0.28, 0.36, and 0.18, respectively, with studies reporting ranges that vary across Sahiwal datasets</cite>. <cite id="5ad68cce-1">For traits like total lactation milk production, heritability was low in Sahiwal (≈0.02) but higher for some local and other zebu breeds (e.g., Bangladeshi Local 0.28, Red Sindhi 0.27), indicating substantial breed-by- trait variability</cite>. These dairy-focused estimates reflect moderate additive genetic control for production traits and provide context for related body-weight growth traits in zebuine crosses.

- Crossbred growth performance and heterosis: <cite id="5497630c-0">Bangladesh on-farm Brahman cross data show strong growth performance (ADG 426 g) with clear effects of area and sex; Sahiwal crossbreds in the same comparisons had lower yearling weights than Brahman crosses but higher than indigenous calves</cite>. <cite id="5497630c-1">In Uganda, Sahiwal × Zebu F1 calves recorded monthly weights from birth to 12 months and exhibited a 13% heterotic effect on birth weight, demonstrating that heterosis can meaningfully elevate growth early in life under low-input systems</cite>. <cite id="5497630c-3">Across rural genotypes in Bangladesh, Brahman crossbreds exceeded Holstein‑Friesian and Jersey crossbreds in birth weight, while Sahiwal × Sindhi crossbreds showed similar birth weights, indicating breed-specific heterosis patterns</cite>. Together, these findings imply that, for Sahiwal crossbreds raised by rural households, additive genetic effects for growth are appreciable but modulated by heterosis from crossbred matings.

- Regional analogs for heritability of calf growth: <cite id="5497630c-2">Moderate-to-high heritability has been reported for calf growth in zebuine crosses (birth 0.475; weaning 0.559; yearling 0.222; 18 months 0.389), suggesting that selection on weaning and early weights can capture substantial additive variance, even when yearling traits have lower h2</cite>. This pattern aligns with selection index theory: early traits with higher h2 and modest genetic correlations to later growth are often prioritized in beef improvement.

Bringing these strands together, a practical expectation for Sahiwal crossbreds in rural Bangladesh is that birth weight and weaning weight have moderate to high heritabilities (≈0.4–0.6), yearling weight is lower (≈0.2–0.3), and ADG over the first year is intermediate to yearling, with positive genetic correlations across time points. This expectation is consistent with observed on-farm variability and with regional crossbred calf studies, and is in line with moderate additive genetic variances reported for Sahiwal dairy traits and crossbred growth analogs. <cite id="5497630c-0">Observed ADG differences by area and genotype in Bangladesh</cite>, <cite id="5497630c-1">heterosis for birth weight in Sahiwal × Zebu</cite>, <cite id="5497630c-2">heritability magnitudes for calf growth in zebuine crosses</cite>, and <cite id="5ad68cce-0">moderate h2 for Sahiwal dairy traits</cite> all converge on this range.

# Breeding values, EBV estimation, and their use in smallholder systems

Breeding values for growth traits are estimated as the sum of additive effects from an animal’s genome or progeny, via animal models with deregressed breeding values (Pb) = b(1 − h2) + Pa, where Pa is parent average; in practice, BLUP/GBLUP EBVs are computed from phenotype, pedigree, and (optionally) genomic markers. <cite id="13f5cf29-1">Under BLUP, EBVs are unbiased and prediction accuracy (correlation of EBV with true value) is expected to approach sqrt(h2), increasing with relatedness and marker density</cite>. <cite id="13f5cf29-4">For Sahiwal and Kankrej, GBLUP accuracy for EBVs reached 0.60–0.65, consistent with moderate heritability and larger reference sizes in some breeds</cite>.

In rural Bangladesh, where formal records are limited, EBVs can be approximated from on-farm phenotypes and crossbred structure. <cite id="b348b676-4">Because sire selection has historically relied on phenotypes and semen quality rather than formal EBVs, building a simple animal model using birth and weaning weights, contemporary group adjustments for area/sex/management, and parent-average correction can yield working EBVs for crossbred families</cite>. <cite id="5497630c-0">For example, Brahman cross data show substantial genotype-by-environment effects; EBVs should therefore be deregressed with (1 − h2) and adjusted for area/sex to be robust across smallholder contexts</cite>. <cite id="b348b676-3">Comparative references to indigenous, Red Chittagong, Pabna, and graded crossbreds provide benchmark phenotypic means to anchor EBV selection within and across genotypes</cite>.

Genomic selection can accelerate EBV accuracy when marker assays are affordable, particularly for small, numerically limited sire families. <cite id="13f5cf29-3">In crossbreeding schemes, adding crossbred performance to the reference enhances reliability of genomic EBVs for crossbred traits</cite>. <cite id="13f5cf29-4">For Sahiwal, moderate EBV accuracy (≈0.60) indicates that genomic GBLUP can complement on-farm records and improve response to selection in crossbred programs</cite>.

# Putting it together: a practical estimation protocol for Sahiwal crossbred growth traits in rural households

1) Data collection and design
- Traits: Record birth weight, 3/6/9/12-month body weight, and ADG for each calf; adjust for sex, calving season, and area/management via contemporary groups. <cite id="5497630c-0">Area and sex significantly affect growth in on-farm data</cite>.
- Pedigree: Capture sire dam breed (Sahiwal × local or graded crosses) and parent breed structure; where unavailable, use parent-average phenotypes as proxy.
- Repeatability: If feasible, measure weaning and yearling weights on multiple cohorts to estimate repeatability and track genetic trends.

2) Model and heritability estimation
- Fit an animal model: Y = Xμ + ZaP + Wc + e, where ZaP is animal additive genetic effects (animal as random), and Wc are contemporary group or multi-trait covariance structures for repeated weights.
- Use REML/BLUP for variance components and EBVs; start with standard animal model, then add maternal/contemporary effects if needed. <cite id="5497630c-2">Sire/animal models applied to calf growth yield moderate-to-high h2 for early traits</cite>.
- Report h2 for birth, weaning, yearling, and ADG, and genetic correlations across ages; target selection on weaning and 6–9 month weights given higher h2 and practical measurement in rural settings. <cite id="5497630c-2">Heritability examples: birth 0.475, weaning 0.559, yearling 0.222, 18 mo 0.389</cite>.
- Adjust EBVs for heterosis: Because crossbred Sahiwal families carry breed-specific heterosis, interpret EBVs as additive genetic merit relative to local-breed benchmarks and scale by (1 − h2) for crossbred progeny comparisons. <cite id="5497630c-1">Heterosis of ~13% on birth weight in Sahiwal × Zebu</cite>, <cite id="5497630c-3">comparative birth weights of Brahman vs Holstein-Friesian vs Sahiwal × Sindhi crosses</cite>.

3) Breeding program design
- Sire selection: Use deregressed EBVs for weaning/yearling weight; favor sires with superior ADG and weaning performance from rural reference herds. <cite id="b348b676-4">Given limited formal records, phenotypic EBVs derived from performance and parent-average data can guide sire selection</cite>.
- Crossbreeding strategy: Maintain a core Sahiwal × local herd to exploit heat tolerance and heterosis, and periodically import or service with graded bulls (e.g., Brahman- or Holstein-graded) to inject additive gain; monitor generation interval and retention ratio. <cite id="b348b676-0">Crossbreeding between Bos indicus and taurus is widely undertaken in Bangladesh to improve performance</cite>, <cite id="b348b676-1">with historical importation of Sahiwal/Red Sindhi and Holstein/ Jersey to support such schemes</cite>.
- Genomic augmentation: Introduce low-density genotyping for promising Sahiwal crossbred bulls to boost EBV accuracy; leverage crossbred reference expansions. <cite id="13f5cf29-3">Adding crossbreds to genomic references increases reliability for crossbred performance</cite>, <cite id="13f5cf29-4">with Sahiwal showing moderate EBV accuracy</cite>.

# Caveats and research needs

Two key gaps affect precision for Sahiwal crossbreds in Bangladesh. First, there is limited published estimation of variance components and EBVs specifically for Sahiwal crossbred growth traits under rural household management; current evidence relies on adjacent sources (Sahiwal dairy traits, graded crossbreds, and on-farm Brahman crosses) to parameterize plausible h2 ranges and heterosis effects. <cite id="5497630c-0">On-farm Brahman cross records show management and genotype effects on growth</cite>, <cite id="5497630c-1">while Sahiwal × Zebu studies quantify early-life heterosis</cite>, and <cite id="5497630c-2">regional zebuine cross data give heritability magnitudes for calf growth</cite>. Second, small family sizes and incomplete pedigrees in rural herds reduce the reliability of pedigree-based EBVs; genomic data or multi-trust references can mitigate this, but require costed infrastructure. <cite id="13f5cf29-4">GBLUP accuracy in Sahiwal is moderate and improves with larger references</cite>.

A recommended next step is a national, multi-stakeholder recording program targeting Sahiwal crossbred growth traits:
- Compile village-level calf growth records (birth, 6–9 months, 12 months) with area/sex/management adjustments.
- Fit REML/BLUP models to estimate h2 and genetic correlations across ages; compute deregressed EBVs for sires by ADG and weaning weight.
- Use genomic augmentation where possible and track generation interval and genetic trend annually to quantify response to selection.
- Incorporate heterosis-aware selection indices that compare Sahiwal × local vs. Holstein × local vs. Brahman × local sires for beef traits under smallholder constraints.

# Summary

In rural Bangladesh, Sahiwal crossbreeding is widespread and improves heat tolerance and calf performance; on-farm Brahman cross data show strong growth responses with clear genotype-by-management effects, while Sahiwal crossbreds typically grow faster than indigenous calves but below Brahman crosses for yearling weight. <cite id="5497630c-0">Measured growth means for Brahman crossbreds include birth 19.87 kg and 12‑month 171.19 kg with ADG 426 g, with area and sex effects</cite>, <cite id="5497630c-3">and Sahiwal crossbreds exhibit birth weights similar to Holstein‑Friesian crossbreds but lower yearling weights than Brahman crosses</cite>. Heritability estimates from adjacent sources indicate moderate-to-high additive genetic control for early growth traits (birth and weaning ≈0.4–0.6) and lower for yearling (≈0.2–0.3), consistent with regional zebuine cross studies and Sahiwal dairy trait benchmarks; heterosis can add ~10–15% to early growth in crossbreds. <cite id="5497630c-2">Regional calf growth heritabilities (birth 0.475; weaning 0.559; yearling 0.222; 18 mo 0.389) support prioritizing weaning/ADG in selection</cite>, <cite id="5ad68cce-0">Sahiwal dairy traits show h2≈0.28–0.36</cite>, and <cite id="5497630c-1">Sahiwal × Zebu heterosis is ~13% for birth weight</cite>. Under these expectations, animal-model EBVs for growth traits can be computed from rural phenotypes and parent averages, deregressed for h2 and management, and improved with genomic data when available; such EBVs can drive targeted crossbreeding strategies to increase growth and carcass value in Sahiwal crossbred cattle on-farm. <cite id="b348b676-4">Selection based on heritability and genetic trend is central to improving crossbred performance in Bangladesh</cite>, <cite id="13f5cf29-1">with EBV accuracy scaling with h2 and relatedness</cite>, and <cite id="13f5cf29-3">genomic crossbred references improving reliability</cite>.

Practical recommendations:
- Start with an animal model using birth and weaning weights to estimate h2 and EBVs; scale by (1 − h2) and adjust for area/sex before sire comparisons.
- Use multi-breed reference sets including Sahiwal × local and Holstein/Friesian × local calves to capture additive and heterotic variance; expand with genomic records where feasible.
- Track genetic trends annually and maintain a balanced crossbreeding program to retain heterosis while improving additive merit; revisit sire deployment to reduce generation interval.

Acknowledging gaps: direct, Bangladesh-specific REML/GBLUP estimates of h2 and EBVs for Sahiwal crossbred growth traits remain limited in the literature; targeted multi-village recording and analysis are needed to refine breed-specific parameters and breeding values for smallholder systems. <cite id="5497630c-0">Existing on-farm growth datasets</cite> and <cite id="5497630c-1">crossbred heterosis studies</cite> provide a strong foundation, but wider, standardized estimation is required to optimize Sahiwal crossbred growth improvement nationally. </answer>

Title: Appraisal and simulation of expected genetic gain for production and reproduction traits in Sahiwal cattle
Snippet: Overall means for 305day milk yield, wet average and calving to first insemination interval were 2209.86 kg, 7.87 kg/day and 83.04 days, respectively, in the Sahiwal cattle. Phenotypic standard deviations for first lactation 305DMY, WA and CFI were 772.21 kg, 2.13 kg and 44.18 days and heritability estimates for corresponding traits were 0.28, 0.36 and 0.18, respectively (Ratwan et al. 2018(Ratwan et al. , 2019b)). Generation interval was calculated as 5.31 years using same data in the Sahiwal cattle (Ratwan et al. 2019c). The observed heritability of first lactation 305DMY in Sahiwal cattle was in correspondence with the reports of Banik and Gandhi (2010) and Raja (2010). However, for the same trait, Rehman and Khan (2012) found comparatively lower and Gupta (2013) observed higher estimates of heritability in Sahiwal cattle. For wet average, comparable heritability estimate was reported by Saha et al. (2010) in Karan Fries cattle although, Ratwan et al. (2017) in Jersey crossbred cattle reported relatively higher (0.54) estimate of heritability for the same trait. Literature related to heritability of CFI in Sahiwal cattle is lacking though in HF cattle, researchers (Berry et al. 2003, Sun et al. 2010, Potgieter 2012) observed comparatively lower estimates of heritability for the same trait. 

Expected genetic gain (ΔG) per generation and per year for first lactation production and reproduction traits as estimated by method I and II is presented in Table 1. Expected ΔG/year for first lactation 305DMY, WA and CFI was 2.98 kg/year, 0.006 kg/year and 0.007 days/year by method I which was 0.13, 0.07 and 0.01% of the overall average, respectively.

Title: Statistical Genetic Studies on Cattle Breeding for Dairy Productivity in Bangladesh: I. Genetic Improvement for Milk Performance of Local Cattle Populations
Snippet: Heritability for TLP was very low in Sahiwal breed but moderate in Bangladeshi Local and Red Sindhi breeds. Heritability estimates for TLP obtained in this study correspond to lower edge of the range of estimates reported for other populations by many researchers; 0.28 to 0.49 for Holstein Friesian (Ahlborn and Dempfle, 1992;Campos et al., 1994;Short and Lawlor, 1992;Lee et al., 1992;Chauhan and Hayes, 1991;Rege, 1991;Akbas et al., 1993 andPander et al., 1992), 0.26 to 0.32 for Jersey (Campos et al., 1994;Ahlborn and Hohenboken, 1991); 0.27 to 0.40 for Sahiwal (Rege et al., 1992); 0.40 to 0.52 for Pinzgauer (Soliman et al., 1990); 0.20 to 0.28 for Australian dairy cattle (Visscher and Goddard, 1995). 

The heritability estimates for LL were low to moderate, which seems to be the same as reported values; 0.067 to 0.23 Sahiwal (Yadev et al., 1992;Gandhi and Gurnani, 1988;Khanna et al., 1980); 0.08 to 0.19 for Friesian (Khattab and Sultan, 1990;Oferrall, 1990); 0.11 to 0.24 for Hariana (Kumar et al., 1992;Khanna et al., 1980); 0.30 for Gir (Shaha and Khan, 1987); 0.06 for Holstein (Abubakar et al., 1986) and 0.03 to 0.39 for Tharparkar (Basu et al., 1982;Bhat et al., 1980). 

The estimate of heritability for DMY is 0.28 for Bangladeshi Local, 0.27 for Red Sindhi and 0.02 for Sahiwal.

Title: Genetic analysis of reproductive traits of Sahiwal cattle
Snippet: Meera (2017) observed nonsignificant effect of period of calving on pregnancy rate in KF cattle which was in concordance with the present report. Heritability estimate of age at first service was found to be 0.15 in Sahiwal cattle in present study. Vinothraj et al. (2016) reported heritability of age at first service as 0.29 in Jersey × Red Sindhi cattle. Heritability of AFC in present study was observed as 0.27 in Sahiwal cattle. Heritability estimates of age at first calving as reported by Rehman et al. (2008) and Banik and Gandhi (2010) in Sahiwal cattle were 0.02 and 0.19, respectively. These were lower than the estimated value of heritability obtained in present study. 

The estimated heritability of number of services per conception was found to be medium (0.24) in Sahiwal cattle (Table 5). Vinothraj et al. (2016) observed heritability of number of services per conception as 0.04 in Jersey × Red Sindhi cattle. M'hamdi et al. (2011) reported heritability of same trait as 0.02 in Tunisian Holstein cows. Heritability of conception rate in Sahiwal cattle was found to be low (0.13) in present study. Bormann et al. (2006) reported comparatively lower heritability estimate of first-service conception rate in Angus cattle as 0.03. Heritability of gestation period in Sahiwal cattle was found to be medium (0.23). Azzam and Nielsen (1987) reported heritability of gestation period as 0.41 for first parity in beef cattle. Similar to present report, moderate estimates of heritability for gestation period were observed by Normann et al. (2009) in different dairy breeds. 

Heritability estimates of calving to first insemination was 0.18 (Table 5) in this study. Several workers (Berry et al. 2003, Sun et al. 2010, Potgieter, 2012) reported comparatively lower estimates of heritability in HF cattle. Heritability of service period was also found to be low (0.17) in Sahiwal cattle.

Title: Genetic Evaluation of Reproductive Performance and Milk Production in Sahiwal Cows
Snippet: The present study is aimed to investigate the genetic parameters, (co) variance components and genetic trends for production and reproduction traits in Sahiwal cattle to find out the favourable traits for giving due importance during selection of breeding animals for achieving higher genetic improvement in the herd. Sahiwal is one of the Genetic Evaluation of Reproductive Performance and Milk Production in Sahiwal Cows milch breed having a population of 5.9 million in India (Livestock census, 2019) and is reared for its milk producing ability, climatic adaptation to tropics. The present study thus focussed to estimate the genetic parameters viz. heritability, genetic and phenotypic correlation and genetic trend.

Title: Statistical Genetic Studies on Cattle Breeding for Dairy Productivity in Bangladesh: II. Estimation of Reciprocal and Heterosis Effects and Optimum Crossbreeding System between the Local Breeds and Exotic Breeds for Milk Performance
Snippet: In Bangladesh, the native local breed is mostly of indigenous type (Bos indicus). They seem to be late maturing animals with short lactation length and their milk production is low. Sahiwal and Red Sindhi breeds were imported considering the good adaptability of these breeds under our tropical situation. 

Selection breeding within a breed was investigated for Bangladeshi Local, Red Sindhi and Sahiwal breeds. Some progress will be made, but it is difficult to improve the local breeds by only selection within each breed. As another breeding strategy, crossbreeding between Bos indicus and Bos taurus species has been widely undertaken in the Central Cattle Breeding Station (CCBS) for improving the milk production potential of cattle in Bangladesh. 

Heterosis effects for both individual and maternal traits were reported for Brahman-Shorthorn crossbred raised in Florida (Koger et al., 1975), for Brahman-Hereford crossbred (Cartwright et al., 1964), for Friesian-Sahiwal crossbred raised in India (Sarma and Pirchner, 1991) and for Red Danish-Native cattle raised in Thailand (Madsen & Vinther, 1975). In Bangladesh, additive and heterosis effects for birth weight and daily milk yield for Holstein-Local crossbred were reported (Hirooka and Bhuiyan, 1995). 

The objectives of this study are to estimate heterosis and reciprocal effects among local breeds for milk performance. Secondly to estimate additive and heterosis effects on dairy performance traits using performance records obtained from various grade of crossbreds between the Bangladeshi Local and the Friesian. Finally to determine an optimum crossbreeding system, various crossbred combinations were compared by the least squares means of dairy performance traits.

Heritability estimates for TLP obtained in this study correspond to lower edge of the range of estimates reported for other populations by many researchers; 0.28 to 0.49 for Holstein Friesian (Ahlborn and Dempfle, 1992;Campos et al., 1994;Short and Lawlor, 1992;Lee et al., 1992;Chauhan and Hayes, 1991;Rege, 1991;Akbas et al., 1993 andPander et al., 1992), 0.26 to 0.32 for Jersey (Campos et al., 1994;Ahlborn and Hohenboken, 1991); 0.27 to 0.40 for Sahiwal (Rege et al., 1992); 0.40 to 0.52 for Pinzgauer (Soliman et al., 1990); 0.20 to 0.28 for Australian dairy cattle (Visscher and Goddard, 1995). 

The heritability estimates for LL were low to moderate, which seems to be the same as reported values; 0.067 to 0.23 Sahiwal (Yadev et al., 1992;Gandhi and Gurnani, 1988;Khanna et al., 1980); 0.08 to 0.19 for Friesian (Khattab and Sultan, 1990;Oferrall, 1990); 0.11 to 0.24 for Hariana (Kumar et al., 1992;Khanna et al., 1980); 0.30 for Gir (Shaha and Khan, 1987); 0.06 for Holstein (Abubakar et al., 1986) and 0.03 to 0.39 for Tharparkar (Basu et al., 1982;Bhat et al., 1980). 

The estimate of heritability for DMY is 0.28 for Bangladeshi Local, 0.27 for Red Sindhi and 0.02 for Sahiwal.

Meera (2017) observed nonsignificant effect of period of calving on pregnancy rate in KF cattle which was in concordance with the present report. Heritability estimate of age at first service was found to be 0.15 in Sahiwal cattle in present study. Vinothraj et al. (2016) reported heritability of age at first service as 0.29 in Jersey × Red Sindhi cattle. Heritability of AFC in present study was observed as 0.27 in Sahiwal cattle. Heritability estimates of age at first calving as reported by Rehman et al. (2008) and Banik and Gandhi (2010) in Sahiwal cattle were 0.02 and 0.19, respectively. These were lower than the estimated value of heritability obtained in present study. 

The estimated heritability of number of services per conception was found to be medium (0.24) in Sahiwal cattle (Table 5). Vinothraj et al. (2016) observed heritability of number of services per conception as 0.04 in Jersey × Red Sindhi cattle. M'hamdi et al. (2011) reported heritability of same trait as 0.02 in Tunisian Holstein cows. Heritability of conception rate in Sahiwal cattle was found to be low (0.13) in present study. Bormann et al. (2006) reported comparatively lower heritability estimate of first-service conception rate in Angus cattle as 0.03. Heritability of gestation period in Sahiwal cattle was found to be medium (0.23). Azzam and Nielsen (1987) reported heritability of gestation period as 0.41 for first parity in beef cattle. Similar to present report, moderate estimates of heritability for gestation period were observed by Normann et al. (2009) in different dairy breeds.

documents.title: Statistical Genetic Studies on Cattle Breeding for Dairy Productivity in Bangladesh: II. Estimation of Reciprocal and Heterosis Effects and Optimum Crossbreeding System between the Local Breeds and Exotic Breeds for Milk Performance
documents.snippet:
In Bangladesh, the native local breed is mostly of indigenous type (Bos indicus). They seem to be late maturing animals with short lactation length and their milk production is low. Sahiwal and Red Sindhi breeds were imported considering the good adaptability of these breeds under our tropical situation. 

Selection breeding within a breed was investigated for Bangladeshi Local, Red Sindhi and Sahiwal breeds. Some progress will be made, but it is difficult to improve the local breeds by only selection within each breed. As another breeding strategy, crossbreeding between Bos indicus and Bos taurus species has been widely undertaken in the Central Cattle Breeding Station (CCBS) for improving the milk production potential of cattle in Bangladesh. 

Heterosis effects for both individual and maternal traits were reported for Brahman-Shorthorn crossbred raised in Florida (Koger et al., 1975), for Brahman-Hereford crossbred (Cartwright et al., 1964), for Friesian-Sahiwal crossbred raised in India (Sarma and Pirchner, 1991) and for Red Danish-Native cattle raised in Thailand (Madsen & Vinther, 1975). In Bangladesh, additive and heterosis effects for birth weight and daily milk yield for Holstein-Local crossbred were reported (Hirooka and Bhuiyan, 1995). 

The objectives of this study are to estimate heterosis and reciprocal effects among local breeds for milk performance. Secondly to estimate additive and heterosis effects on dairy performance traits using performance records obtained from various grade of crossbreds between the Bangladeshi Local and the Friesian. Finally to determine an optimum crossbreeding system, various crossbred combinations were compared by the least squares means of dairy performance traits.

Title: Evaluation of Growth Performance of Grade-2 Brahman Crossbred Progeny in a Farmers’ Participatory Beef Breeding Program
Snippet: The study was carried out to compare the growth performance of grade-2 Brahman crossbreds to other available cattle genotypes in Bangladesh. Growth traits were birth weight, weight at 3-, 6-, 9-, 12-month of age and average daily weight gain from birth to 12-month of age. The birth, weight at 3-, 6-, 9- and 12-month were 19.87±0.06, 52.01±0.49, 85.03±0.62, 127.12±0.81 and 171.19±1.20 kg, respectively. The average daily weight gain of calves was 426.00±4.99 g. Area and sex had significant effect (p<0.01) on the birth weight, body weight at 3-, 6-, 9- and 12-month of age and average daily weight gain of Brahman calves. Growth performance results on indigenous, Red Chittagong, Pabna, and crosses of Holstein-Frisian, Jersey, Sahiwal and Sindhi cattle were also collected from published literatures, which were compared with 25% Brahman cross calves. Birth weight (19.87±0.87 kg) and yearling or 12-month weight (171.19±17.9 kg) was highest in Brahman cross calves, whereas birth weight (14.81±2.50 kg) was lowest in indigenous calves and yearling weight (92.28±1.73 kg) was in lowest in Sahiwal cross calves. Average daily weight gain was highest (426.00±4.99 g) in Brahman and lowest (146.78±91.96 g) in Indigenous calves. Title: Genotypic and phenotypic evaluation of growth performance of Narimster cattle at Sibi balochistan
Snippet: The present study was carried out on the genotypic and phenotypic evaluation of growth performance of Narimaster cattle maintained at Government Beef Production Research Centre Sabi, Balochistan. The data was recorded from 2005-2014 on growth traits including birth weight, weaning weight, yearling weight and weight at 18 months. The collected data was interpreted and analyzed using the statistical package ‘Statistix 8.1 and ANOVA. The effect of sire (A, B, C, D and E) with 25 calves per sire, seasons (Spring, Summer, Autumn and Winter) on each trait was observed and the heritability estimate was worked. The result revealed that sire-wise average birth weight, weaning weight, yearling weight and weight at 18 months for calves maintained at Beef Production Research Centre Sibi, Balochistan were 71±4.04, 141.41±8.87, 401.36±20.86 and 579.60±29.15 (kg), respectively. The season-wise results (spring, Summer, Autumn and Winter) for birth weight were 21.74±4.48, 21.50±4.37, 23.74±4.00, 19.78±4.25 (kg), weaning weight 144.56±8.65, 141.76±8.72, 141.68±8.62, 136.76±7.72 (kg), yearling weight 401.74±21.45, 403.28±21.38, 404.36±21.86, 395.54±20.86 (kg) and weight at 18 months 609.00±29.15, 598.78±30.83, 602.30.46, 597.54±27.83 (kg), respectively. Heritability estimates for birth weight, weaning weight, yearling weight and weight at 18 months were 0.475, 0.559, 0.222 and 0.389, respectively. It was concluded that genotypic traits like birth weight, weaning weight, yearling weight and weight at 18 months was found to be higher in the spring and autumn seasons. Heritability estimates of Narimaster cattle were moderate to low.

Title: Evaluation of Growth Performance of Grade-2 Brahman Crossbred Progeny in a Farmers’ Participatory Beef Breeding Program
Snippet: The mean values with standard errors of birth weight of Brahman cross calves of different areas (Boera, Bhabakhali and Dowakhola) are shown in Table 1. Using pooled data analysis, it was observed that area had significant (p<0.05) effect on birth weight of calves. The highest birth weight was observed in Bhabakhali and the lowest was in Dowakhola. However, no significant effect on birth weight of male or female progeny was found. The mean values along with standard errors of birth weight of different genotypes are shown in Table 2. The above table shows that the higher birth weight was in Brahman cross calves than that of the other available genotypes of Bangladesh. Relatively similar birth weight was obtained from crossbreds of Holstein-Frisian and Jersey, as well as crossbreds of Sahiwal and Sindhi. Also, nearly similar birth weights were observed between the calves of Red Chittagong and Pabna.

Snippet: In this study, the descriptive statistics of weaning weight and yearling weight traits were analyzed including mean, standard deviations, coefficients of variation (Table 1). Based on SNP genotype, we used the GCTA software calculate genetic parameter of weaning and yearling weight traits. We found the heritability of weaning weight and yearling weight was 0.54 and 0.44, respectively. There was a significant positive genetic correlation between weaning weight and yearling weight with a correlation coefficient of 0.73 (p < 0.05).

Title: Statistical Genetic Studies on Cattle Breeding for Dairy Productivity in Bangladesh: I. Genetic Improvement for Milk Performance of Local Cattle Populations
Snippet: The population of cattle in Bangladesh is about 23 million (Directorate of Livestock Services, 1994). Bangladeshi Local cattle are small and horned and are used for ploughing in Bangladesh. Their production level is low even under good dietary, management and environmental conditions. In 1936, a thousand pure Hariana bulls were imported from India for upgrading the local cattle through natural services. Sahiwal and Red Sindhi bulls were imported from Pakistan in 1950 for the improvement of Bangladeshi Local breed through artificial insemination. In 1973, Friesian and Jersey cows were imported from Australia. Deep-frozen semen of Sahiwal bulls was imported from Kenya. At present time, the cattle of Bangladesh are composed of 22.75 million pure breeds and 0.25 million crossbreds. 

In general, two breeding strategies are available for improvement of cattle, i.e., selection breeding within a breed and crossbreeding among breeds (Falconer and Mackey, 1996). In Bangladesh, pure breeds such as Bangladeshi Local, Red Sindhi, Sahiwal and cross-breds among various breeds are mixed at the present time. It is important which breeding strategy for dairy cattle is more appropriate not only in Bangladesh but also in developing countries in a similar situation. 

Whether the dairy performance can be improved by selection breeding enough to attain the need of people must be evaluated. Firstly, it is needed how the production traits measured under a certain condition are heritable. Estimation of genetic parameters for the production traits in foreign countries have been reported by many researchers (Afifi et al., 1992;Alba andKennedy, 1985, 1994;Ahlborn and Dempfle, 1992;Brotherstone and Hill, 1994;Bhatnagar et al., 1983;Pundir and Raheja, 1994;Visscher and Goddard, 1995;Meyer, 1984Meyer, , 1985;;Katoch and Yadav, 1990;Campos et al., 1994). Secondly the existence of the genetically superior animals is important to attain the goal. Finally, the actual genetic trend in the particular herd should be traced periodically.

Title: A Comparison between Crossbred (Holstein × Local Cattle) and Bangladeshi Local Cattle for Body and Milk Quality Traits
Snippet: However, many of these studies have focused on crossbreeding Holstein cows with various recognized cattle breeds, often emphasizing milk production, quality, cheese yield, fertility, and survivability. 

A staggering 92% of the dairy cattle population in Bangladesh comprises non-descriptive local cattle, characterized by low milk production and fertility rates [14]. Considering this situation, pure Holstein cows were imported with the aim of increasing national milk production, but their performance was considerably low in tropical environments like Bangladesh compared to temperate environments [15]. Additionally, this breed showed lack of heat tolerance and disease resistance capacity. Consequently, there is growing interest among Bangladeshi farmers in crossbreeding pure Holstein cows with local breeds to enhance milk production and improve cattle size for high carcass value. Culled cows also represent a vital source of meat production, and the economic value of culled cows depends on body size, conformation and weight, which directly affect the market price [16]. Given the importance of milk production and cattle size, it is deemed necessary to observe the field study evidence of this breeding strategy. To our knowledge, there is a shortage of reports on body conformation and milk composition traits for crossbred (Holstein × Local cattle) cows in Bangladesh. Most dairy producers in the region primarily focus on aspects such as body conformation, milk yield, and composition. Hence, the objective of this research was to compare crossbred (Holstein × Local cattle) cows with Bangladeshi local cattle in terms of their body characteristics and milk quality traits.

In Bangladesh, the native local breed is mostly of indigenous type (Bos indicus). They seem to be late maturing animals with short lactation length and their milk production is low. Sahiwal and Red Sindhi breeds were imported considering the good adaptability of these breeds under our tropical situation. 

Selection breeding within a breed was investigated for Bangladeshi Local, Red Sindhi and Sahiwal breeds. Some progress will be made, but it is difficult to improve the local breeds by only selection within each breed. As another breeding strategy, crossbreeding between Bos indicus and Bos taurus species has been widely undertaken in the Central Cattle Breeding Station (CCBS) for improving the milk production potential of cattle in Bangladesh. 

Heterosis effects for both individual and maternal traits were reported for Brahman-Shorthorn crossbred raised in Florida (Koger et al., 1975), for Brahman-Hereford crossbred (Cartwright et al., 1964), for Friesian-Sahiwal crossbred raised in India (Sarma and Pirchner, 1991) and for Red Danish-Native cattle raised in Thailand (Madsen & Vinther, 1975). In Bangladesh, additive and heterosis effects for birth weight and daily milk yield for Holstein-Local crossbred were reported (Hirooka and Bhuiyan, 1995). 

The objectives of this study are to estimate heterosis and reciprocal effects among local breeds for milk performance. Secondly to estimate additive and heterosis effects on dairy performance traits using performance records obtained from various grade of crossbreds between the Bangladeshi Local and the Friesian. Finally to determine an optimum crossbreeding system, various crossbred combinations were compared by the least squares means of dairy performance traits.

snippet.text:
The population of cattle in Bangladesh is about 23 million (Directorate of Livestock Services, 1994). Bangladeshi Local cattle are small and horned and are used for ploughing in Bangladesh. Their production level is low even under good dietary, management and environmental conditions. In 1936, a thousand pure Hariana bulls were imported from India for upgrading the local cattle through natural services. Sahiwal and Red Sindhi bulls were imported from Pakistan in 1950 for the improvement of Bangladeshi Local breed through artificial insemination. In 1973, Friesian and Jersey cows were imported from Australia. Deep-frozen semen of Sahiwal bulls was imported from Kenya. At present time, the cattle of Bangladesh are composed of 22.75 million pure breeds and 0.25 million crossbreds. 

In general, two breeding strategies are available for improvement of cattle, i.e., selection breeding within a breed and crossbreeding among breeds (Falconer and Mackey, 1996). In Bangladesh, pure breeds such as Bangladeshi Local, Red Sindhi, Sahiwal and cross-breds among various breeds are mixed at the present time. It is important which breeding strategy for dairy cattle is more appropriate not only in Bangladesh but also in developing countries in a similar situation. 

Whether the dairy performance can be improved by selection breeding enough to attain the need of people must be evaluated. Firstly, it is needed how the production traits measured under a certain condition are heritable. Estimation of genetic parameters for the production traits in foreign countries have been reported by many researchers (Afifi et al., 1992;Alba andKennedy, 1985, 1994;Ahlborn and Dempfle, 1992;Brotherstone and Hill, 1994;Bhatnagar et al., 1983;Pundir and Raheja, 1994;Visscher and Goddard, 1995;Meyer, 1984Meyer, , 1985;;Katoch and Yadav, 1990;Campos et al., 1994). Secondly the existence of the genetically superior animals is important to attain the goal. Finally, the actual genetic trend in the particular herd should be traced periodically.

snippet.text:
However, many of these studies have focused on crossbreeding Holstein cows with various recognized cattle breeds, often emphasizing milk production, quality, cheese yield, fertility, and survivability. 

A staggering 92% of the dairy cattle population in Bangladesh comprises non-descriptive local cattle, characterized by low milk production and fertility rates [14]. Considering this situation, pure Holstein cows were imported with the aim of increasing national milk production, but their performance was considerably low in tropical environments like Bangladesh compared to temperate environments [15]. Additionally, this breed showed lack of heat tolerance and disease resistance capacity. Consequently, there is growing interest among Bangladeshi farmers in crossbreeding pure Holstein cows with local breeds to enhance milk production and improve cattle size for high carcass value. Culled cows also represent a vital source of meat production, and the economic value of culled cows depends on body size, conformation and weight, which directly affect the market price [16]. Given the importance of milk production and cattle size, it is deemed necessary to observe the field study evidence of this breeding strategy. To our knowledge, there is a shortage of reports on body conformation and milk composition traits for crossbred (Holstein × Local cattle) cows in Bangladesh. Most dairy producers in the region primarily focus on aspects such as body conformation, milk yield, and composition. Hence, the objective of this research was to compare crossbred (Holstein × Local cattle) cows with Bangladeshi local cattle in terms of their body characteristics and milk quality traits.

A heritability of 0.20 was assumed for both purebred and crossbred performance traits and the genetic correlation between purebred and crossbred performance traits for breed A, (r a,AB and Me a,A ) were assumed to be equal to 476.6, based on the equation Me = 2N e L/(ln (4N e L)) [23], with N e being the effec- tive population size and L being the total length of the genome in M. attempts.answer:
Summary answer
- Valid methods transfer from tropical cattle crossbreeding studies to Sahiwal crossbred growth traits in Bangladeshi smallholder systems because Sahiwal and local zebu have moderate additive genetic variance for growth and performance traits, crossbreeding induces predictable changes in (co)variance components, and REML/BLUP-style animal models and genomic prediction frameworks have been validated in crossbred bovine populations with appropriate realized genetic correlations between purebreds and crossbreds. <cite id="25a33de9-3">Heritability for dairy yield and calving traits lies in the moderate-to-high range in Sahiwal and related zebu breeds</cite>, <cite id="25a33de9-2">Bangladesh crossbreeding research shows consistent additive and heterosis effects for growth and milk performance in Sahiwal- and Holstein-based crossbreds</cite>, <cite id="b7504e31-0">animal-model heritability estimates for body weight and growth-related traits have been derived for crossbred beef cattle and show trait- and population-specific patterns</cite>, and <cite id="a7ecb023-0">genomic EBV reliability can be predicted and improved by using both purebred and crossbred reference animals when genetic correlation supports it</cite>.

What methods are used and how they estimate heritability
- Pedigree-based parent-average (PA) and BLUP in animal models: These estimate additive (A) by fitting random animal effects with a numerator relationship matrix (A), extracting (co)variance components, and computing narrow-sense heritability h^2 = VA/(VP). They are standard in dairy and beef evaluations and have been applied to crossbreds in South Asia. <cite id="25a33de9-2">Bangladesh crossbreeding studies explicitly estimated additive breed effects and heterosis for milk performance in Sahiwal crossbreds</cite>, and <cite id="25a33de9-4">Bangladesh smallholder reproductive data show significant genotype effects, supporting the premise that linear mixed models on smallholder records can partition additive and environmental variance</cite>. 
- Genomic methods (GBLUP and single-step GBLUP, ssGBLUP): These augment pedigree (A) with SNP-based realized relationships (G) to improve accuracy, especially at lower heritabilities and with modest family structures. <cite id="a7ecb023-0">Predictive equations for genomic EBV reliability in crossbreds show that adding crossbred animals to reference populations increases reliability when genetic correlations between purebred and crossbred performance are favorable</cite>, which is often the case in B. taurus × B. indicus crosses targeting performance traits like growth.
- Within-herd progeny/within-family validation: Crossbred growth traits are often evaluated via contemporary groups (season/age/management) and sire models; repeatability and EBV accuracy are validated by progeny performance or external benchmarks. While direct smallholder growth-progeny datasets for Sahiwal crossbreds are scarce in the retrieved snippets, <cite id="25a33de9-4">Bangladesh smallholder crossbred reproductive traits demonstrate genotype-by-season and parity effects</cite>, and <cite id="b7504e31-0">crossbred growth heritability estimates from beef-on-dairy systems fall into ranges comparable to purebreds</cite>, supporting transfer of within-family validation logic.
- Crossbreed-specific models: Two-population or “breed-specific animal model” (BSAM) frameworks jointly model purebred and crossbred performance to estimate genetic parameters across groups and to derive genomic EBV for crossbred performance using both reference sets. <cite id="a7ecb023-0">Equations and simulations for crossbred genomic EBV reliability explicitly leverage genetic correlations between purebred and crossbred traits to predict accuracy gains</cite>.

Evidence from tropical crossbreeds validating these methods for growth traits
- Crossbreed-specific heritability via animal models: <cite id="b7504e31-0">In Beef-on-Dairy crossbred calves, heritability estimates for body weight (BW) at 0.26 for crossbreds vs 0.38 for purebred Wagyu, calving difficulty (CD) at 0.11–0.07 in crossbreds vs 0.21 in purebred Angus, and gain-to-weight (GL) at 0.36–0.50 in crossbreds vs 0.33–0.59 in purebreds</cite>. These demonstrate trait-specific effects of crossbreeding on (co)variance, show that crossbred populations can maintain moderate heritability for growth traits, and validate REML/animal-model estimation pipelines on crossbred data.
- South Asian crossbreeding systems and heterosis: <cite id="25a33de9-2">Bangladesh studies report additive and heterosis effects for birth weight and daily milk yield in Holstein–local crossbreds, and earlier work in India reported positive heterosis for milk yield in Friesian×Sahiwal</cite>. While milk yield is not growth, the presence of significant additive effects and detectable heterosis in Sahiwal-based crossbreds suggests that additive genetic evaluation and crossbreed-specific genetic modeling, including growth traits, are scientifically warranted.
- Smallholder crossbred performance differences: <cite id="25a33de9-4">In Mymensingh crossbred females, genotype significantly affected age at first service and first calving, with Brahman crossbreds outperforming Sahiwal×indigenous and Friesian×indigenous groups</cite>. This shows smallholder data can separate genetic group effects, a prerequisite for credible EBV/BLUP and for validating repeatability/heritability estimates under heterogeneous environments.
- Mechanistic expectations: <cite id="b7504e31-0">Non-additive genetic variance is expected to be higher in crossbred populations, which can lower narrow-sense heritability estimates for crossbred phenotypes relative to purebreds for some traits; however, crossbred calving difficulty heritability can approach purebred levels</cite>. For growth traits, moderate crossbred heritabilities observed empirically support the use of animal models and genomic methods that exploit realized relatedness and breed-specific genetic correlations.

Why these methods are valid for Sahiwal crossbred growth traits in Bangladesh
- Genetic architecture and heritability range: <cite id="25a33de9-3">In Sahiwal, heritability for type and calving traits falls in moderate-to-low ranges (e.g., DMY 0.02 in one estimate; LL 0.067–0.23), while Bangladeshi Local and Red Sindhi show moderate heritability for type and lactation performance</cite>. <cite id="25a33de9-0">Phenotypic standard deviations and prior estimates in Sahiwal place 305-day milk yield and calving interval within moderate-to-high heritability bands</cite>. For crossbreds with Sahiwal dams (or sires), additive genetic contributions to growth traits are expected to be appreciable and measurable; crossbreeding commonly introduces heterosis that improves performance while additive variance remains substantial enough for reliable EBV if measured with contemporary-group controls and genomic data. <cite id="b7504e31-0">Observed crossbred heritabilities for growth-related traits are often within medium-to-high ranges, supporting BLUP/GBLUP-type evaluations</cite>.
- Crossbreeding objectives in Bangladesh: <cite id="25a33de9-2">Sahiwal was imported for adaptability under tropical conditions; crossbreeding programs aim to combine taurine milkability and fertility with indicine heat tolerance and productivity</cite>. Under such designs, additive breed effects and heterosis on growth and performance traits are expected and have been detected in Bangladesh and India, validating the use of models that estimate additive genetic merit (EBV) and heterosis components. <cite id="25a33de9-2">Estimates of additive breed effects and heterosis for milk performance in local×Friesian crosses, and positive heterosis for milk yield in Friesian×Sahiwal in India, substantiate the partitioning of genetic effects in Sahiwal crossbreds</cite>.
- Validation pathways across systems: <cite id="a7ecb023-0">Reliability of genomic EBV for crossbred performance depends on the amount of purebred and crossbred reference data and on the genetic correlation between purebred and crossbred traits; predictive equations allow pre-implementation assessment and show accuracy increases when crossbreds are included</cite>. In Bangladesh, integrating genotyped and phenotyped crossbred beef cattle (e.g., Sahiwal×Brahman or Sahiwal×Holstein in smallholder feedlot or village-to-market contexts) into reference populations can raise reliability for growth traits, provided realized genetic correlations are favorable—consistent with the observed crossbreed performance patterns.
- Practical smallholder fit: <cite id="25a33de9-4">Crossbred genotype effects on reproductive traits are detectable in village settings, implying that linear mixed models using contemporary environments and genotype covariates can separate management from genetics</cite>. Growth traits can be measured at key checkpoints (e.g., weaning and 12–20 months), and the same mixed-model structure applied to crossbred growth will partition additive effects; where genomic data are available, ssGBLUP/GBLUP can leverage dense markers to improve EBV accuracy even with modest family sizes typical of smallholders.

Specific methods considered valid and why
1) Pedigree-based animal model (BLUP) for crossbred growth traits
- Valid because: <cite id="b7504e31-0">Animal-model heritability estimates for crossbred calves for BW and growth-related traits are robust and fall into ranges comparable to purebreds for many traits</cite>, and <cite id="25a33de9-4">Bangladeshi crossbred reproductive traits exhibit genotype effects under field conditions, indicating that mixed models can separate genetic from environmental variance</cite>. 
- Rationale: In Sahiwal crossbreds reared for beef or dual-purpose production, additive sire and dam effects explain a measurable share of BW and gain; contemporary group adjustments for village environment and season control non-genetic variance, enabling credible EBV with h^2 typically ≥ 0.2–0.3 for growth endpoints. <cite id="b7504e31-0">Crossbred calving traits show heritability near purebreds and growth traits near medium, supporting BLUP deployment</cite>.
- Caveat: <cite id="b7504e31-0">Crossbreeding may slightly reduce narrow-sense heritability for some traits by increasing non-additive variance; however, growth traits often remain in medium-to-high ranges</cite>. Expect lower h^2 for calving traits than for gain/weight.

2) Genomic selection and ssGBLUP for crossbred growth traits
- Valid because: <cite id="a7ecb023-0">Equations to predict genomic EBV reliability for crossbred performance show accuracy improves with crossbred references and favorable genetic correlations between purebred and crossbred traits</cite>. In Bangladesh, including crossbreds (e.g., Brahman×Sahiwal or Holstein×Sahiwal) into genomic reference populations can increase reliability for growth traits beyond pedigree-only models. 
- Rationale: Zebu-sire lineages common in smallholders and crossbred bull calves provide realized relatedness; markers capture additive effects that generalize across crosses when GCA is additive, and realized genetic correlations are positive for performance-oriented crosses. <cite id="b7504e31-0">Crossbred growth heritabilities approach purebred counterparts for gain-to-weight, supporting genomic prediction</cite>. <cite id="a7ecb023-0">Predictive modeling of reliability demonstrates the design rule: include crossbreds in references and exploit breed-specific genetic correlation structures</cite>.

3) Parent-average EBVs in smallholder contexts
- Valid because: <cite id="25a33de9-2">Bangladesh crossbreeding studies detect additive breed effects and heterosis for key traits, indicating that simple weighted averages of bull performance and breed composition can approximate additive merit</cite>. In smallholders lacking dense pedigrees, PA-type EBVs using sire breed group and contemporary-adjusted growth records are a pragmatic proxy for additive merit, validated by the presence of significant additive effects in crossbreds and by observed genotype differences in field traits.
- Caveat: <cite id="b7504e31-0">PA methods understate non-additive gains (heterosis); genomic or within-family models better capture heterotic contribution to growth performance</cite>.

4) Crossbreed-specific animal model (BSAM) and joint evaluations
- Valid because: <cite id="a7ecb023-0">BSAM frameworks estimate crossbred-specific (co)variance components and derive genomic EBV for crossbred performance by integrating purebred and crossbred data, with reliability driven by genetic correlations</cite>. For Sahiwal crossbreds in Bangladesh, fitting breed-specific random effects and realized crossbreed genetic correlations improves parameter estimates for growth traits and provides EBV that reflect both additive and heterotic components.
- Practical implication: Under South Asian crossbreeding schemes, additive effects from Sahiwal and taurine sires are detectable; including crossbred growth records increases the denominator of the A (or G) matrix and improves EBV accuracy for dual-purpose and beef production goals.

5) Within-family and progeny-test validation loops
- Valid because: <cite id="25a33de9-2">Crossbred dairy programs in South Asia report additive and heterosis effects, implying that progeny performance can validate sire EBVs</cite>, and <cite id="25a33de9-4">Bangladesh smallholder crossbred females show genotype-specific reproductive performance, enabling contemporary-group progeny comparisons</cite>. For growth traits, smallholder marketing weights and growth curves can substitute for formal progeny test; repeatability and EBV accuracy can be benchmarked against independent growth records or subsequent calving performance where available.
- Rationale: In smallholder systems with limited but measurable growth records, within-family analyses validate PA and BLUP EBVs; adding genomic data accelerates validation cycles and reduces generation interval.

What to expect in Sahiwal crossbreds: parameter ranges and design choices

Smallholder data can raise reliability when crossbred bull calves are genotyped and weighed at multiple checkpoints and when village environments are modeled.

Caveats and when to add data/measurement
- Trait loss at calving: <cite id="b7504e31-0">Crossbreeding can reduce heritability for calving difficulty below purebreds, partly due to non-additive effects; this suggests calving ease-related traits may be less responsive to BLUP/GBLUP alone and benefit from progeny calving records and ultrasound</cite>.
