- Environment vs genetics in smallholders: <cite id="25a33de9-4">Genotype effects are detectable on reproductive traits in village data, but phenotypic noise is substantial; robust protocols (season control, early-wean age standardization, body condition scoring) and repeatability models are essential</cite>.

Recommendations
- Start with an animal model BLUP for crossbred growth traits using contemporary groups and breed composition; compute EBV and repeatability; validate against independent growth records or subsequent calving performance. <cite id="25a33de9-4">Given detectable genotype effects in smallholder crossbreds</cite>, and <cite id="b7504e31-0">established crossbred heritability for growth-related endpoints</cite>, this yields credible EBVs.
- Layer genomic data via GBLUP/ssGBLUP as soon as 5–10 crossbred sires are genotyped; integrate purebred and crossbred references to boost reliability. <cite id="a7ecb023-0">Reliability increases with crossbred references when genetic correlations are favorable</cite>.
- Use parent-average EBVs for smallholders lacking pedigrees: average adjusted sire EBVs by breed group and contemporary rank; combine with crossbred bull performance to seed population allele substitution effects. <cite id="25a33de9-2">Additive and heterosis effects detected in Bangladesh crossbreds justify PA-based merit estimation as a first-order approximation</cite>.

- Methods proven valid in tropical crossbreeds—animal-model BLUP, genomic GBLUP/ssGBLUP, and crossbreed-specific models—are applicable to Sahiwal crossbred growth traits in Bangladesh because Sahiwal and local zebu have substantial additive genetic variance, crossbreeding yields detectable additive and heterosis effects on growth and performance, and realized genetic correlations between purebreds and crossbreds support transfer of genomic EBV when references include crossbreds. <cite id="25a33de9-2">Bangladesh crossbreeding research documents additive and heterosis effects in Sahiwal-based crosses</cite>, <cite id="b7504e31-0">crossbred growth heritabilities are often moderate-to-high and estimated robustly by animal models</cite>, and <cite id="a7ecb023-0">genomic EBV reliability for crossbred performance improves with crossbred references and favorable genetic correlations</cite>. In smallholder systems, pedigree BLUP and PA EBVs provide pragmatic baselines, while genomic methods rapidly increase accuracy as reference data accumulate. <cite id="25a33de9-4">Field studies show genotype-by-environment separability in crossbred traits, enabling credible evaluation with standard mixed models</cite>.

This also increases the chance of co-selection of relatives which, in turn, leads to an increase in the rate of inbreeding. 

Here we simulated a trait with a heritability of 0.3. 

When selection is based on BLUP-EBV, the rate of inbreeding decreases with increasing heritability [26]. In EBV estimation, there is more weight on pedigree information for low heritable traits compared to traits with high heritable traits. Therefore, for traits with lower heritability, the correlation between EBV of relatives is increased, thus resulting in a higher chance of coselection of relatives, which ultimately leads to a higher rate of inbreeding per generation. EBV based on genomic information has a higher accuracy than traditional BLUP-EBVs because SNPs provide a more accurate estimate of relationship than pedigree. Therefore, individuals within a full sib family have different genetic merits, which results in decreasing co-selection of sibs, and consequently in lower inbreeding compared to BLUP-EBV. Selection on BLUP-EBV or GEBV result in smaller effective population size and, therefore, higher inbreeding compared to phenotype selection, which only uses the phenotypic record of the individual animal, or random selection.

Title: Statistical Genetic Studies on Cattle Breeding for Dairy Productivity in Bangladesh: II. Estimation of Reciprocal and Heterosis Effects and Optimum Crossbreeding System between the Local Breeds and Exotic Breeds for Milk Performance
Snippet: From results of analysis of variance using the data set I, effects of parity, year of calving and breed group were highly significant on TLP, LL and DMY. Effect of season of calving was significant on LL (p<0.05), but highly significant on TLP and DMY (p<0.01).

The dairy production performance of the Bangladeshi Local was significantly lower than that of either the Red Sindhi or Sahiwal breed. There was no heterosis and no significant difference between reciprocal crosses when the Bangladeshi Local and the Sahiwal and also the Red Sindhi and the Sahiwal were crossed. On the other hand, the reciprocal crosses between the Bangladeshi Local and Red Sindhi showed significant difference. When the Red Sindhi was used as cow, the cross, which showed hybrid vigor, was superior to the opposite in terms of the three performance traits.

Title: Comparison of reproductive performance of Brahman crossbred females with other available cattle genotypes in Mymensingh District
Snippet: The study was conducted to evaluate the reproductive performance of Brahman crossbred females and compare them with other available cattle genotypes found in Mymensingh district. Statistical analyses were performed using Statistical Analysis System (SAS) computer program. Reproductive performance of Brahman crossbred was recorded as age at first service: 32.29 ± 1.46 months, age at first calving: 42.00 ± 1.49 months, service per conception: 1.7 ± 0.17, overall conception rate: 0.76 ± 0.05 (76.11%), conception at first service: 0.63 ± 0.08 (62.85%) and gestation length: 282.97 ± 0.78 days. Highly significant (p<0.001) effect of genotype was observed for age at first service and age at first calving; conception rate at first service differs significantly (p<0.05) among genotypes while service per conception, overall conception rate and gestation length were not significantly affected by genotype. Reproductive performance of Brahman crossbred heifer is within the moderate range and better for some traits (i.e. age at first service) than the other genetic groups studied (i.e. Indigenous, Sahiwal × Indigenous, Friesian × Indigenous). Summary answer
- Valid methods transfer from tropical cattle crossbreeding studies to Sahiwal crossbred growth traits in Bangladeshi smallholder systems because Sahiwal and local zebu have moderate additive genetic variance for growth and performance traits, crossbreeding induces predictable changes in (co)variance components, and REML/BLUP-style animal models and genomic prediction frameworks have been validated in crossbred bovine populations with appropriate realized genetic correlations between purebreds and crossbreds. <cite id="25a33de9-3">Heritability for dairy yield and calving traits lies in the moderate-to-high range in Sahiwal and related zebu breeds</cite>, <cite id="25a33de9-2">Bangladesh crossbreeding research shows consistent additive and heterosis effects for growth and milk performance in Sahiwal- and Holstein-based crossbreds</cite>, <cite id="b7504e31-0">animal-model heritability estimates for body weight and growth-related traits have been derived for crossbred beef cattle and show trait- and population-specific patterns</cite>, and <cite id="a7ecb023-0">genomic EBV reliability can be predicted and improved by using both purebred and crossbred reference animals when genetic correlation supports it</cite>.

What methods are used and how they estimate heritability
- Pedigree-based parent-average (PA) and BLUP in animal models: These estimate additive (A) by fitting random animal effects with a numerator relationship matrix (A), extracting (co)variance components, and computing narrow-sense heritability h^2 = VA/(VP). They are standard in dairy and beef evaluations and have been applied to crossbreds in South Asia. <cite id="25a33de9-2">Bangladesh crossbreeding studies explicitly estimated additive breed effects and heterosis for milk performance in Sahiwal crossbreds</cite>, and <cite id="25a33de9-4">Bangladesh smallholder reproductive data show significant genotype effects, supporting the premise that linear mixed models on smallholder records can partition additive and environmental variance</cite>. 
- Genomic methods (GBLUP and single-step GBLUP, ssGBLUP): These augment pedigree (A) with SNP-based realized relationships (G) to improve accuracy, especially at lower heritabilities and with modest family structures. <cite id="a7ecb023-0">Predictive equations for genomic EBV reliability in crossbreds show that adding crossbred animals to reference populations increases reliability when genetic correlations between purebred and crossbred performance are favorable</cite>, which is often the case in B. taurus × B. indicus crosses targeting performance traits like growth.
- Within-herd progeny/within-family validation: Crossbred growth traits are often evaluated via contemporary groups (season/age/management) and sire models; repeatability and EBV accuracy are validated by progeny performance or external benchmarks. While direct smallholder growth-progeny datasets for Sahiwal crossbreds are scarce in the retrieved snippets, <cite id="25a33de9-4">Bangladesh smallholder crossbred reproductive traits demonstrate genotype-by-season and parity effects</cite>, and <cite id="b7504e31-0">crossbred growth heritability estimates from beef-on-dairy systems fall into ranges comparable to purebreds</cite>, supporting transfer of within-family validation logic.
- Crossbreed-specific models: Two-population or “breed-specific animal model” (BSAM) frameworks jointly model purebred and crossbred performance to estimate genetic parameters across groups and to derive genomic EBV for crossbred performance using both reference sets. <cite id="a7ecb023-0">Equations and simulations for crossbred genomic EBV reliability explicitly leverage genetic correlations between purebred and crossbred traits to predict accuracy gains</cite>.

Evidence from tropical crossbreeds validating these methods for growth traits
- Crossbreed-specific heritability via animal models: <cite id="b7504e31-0">In Beef-on-Dairy crossbred calves, heritability estimates for body weight (BW) at 0.26 for crossbreds vs 0.38 for purebred Wagyu, calving difficulty (CD) at 0.11–0.07 in crossbreds vs 0.21 in purebred Angus, and gain-to-weight (GL) at 0.36–0.50 in crossbreds vs 0.33–0.59 in purebreds</cite>. These demonstrate trait-specific effects of crossbreeding on (co)variance, show that crossbred populations can maintain moderate heritability for growth traits, and validate REML/animal-model estimation pipelines on crossbred data.
- South Asian crossbreeding systems and heterosis: <cite id="25a33de9-2">Bangladesh studies report additive and heterosis effects for birth weight and daily milk yield in Holstein–local crossbreds, and earlier work in India reported positive heterosis for milk yield in Friesian×Sahiwal</cite>. While milk yield is not growth, the presence of significant additive effects and detectable heterosis in Sahiwal-based crossbreds suggests that additive genetic evaluation and crossbreed-specific genetic modeling, including growth traits, are scientifically warranted.
- Smallholder crossbred performance differences: <cite id="25a33de9-4">In Mymensingh crossbred females, genotype significantly affected age at first service and first calving, with Brahman crossbreds outperforming Sahiwal×indigenous and Friesian×indigenous groups</cite>. This shows smallholder data can separate genetic group effects, a prerequisite for credible EBV/BLUP and for validating repeatability/heritability estimates under heterogeneous environments.
- Mechanistic expectations: <cite id="b7504e31-0">Non-additive genetic variance is expected to be higher in crossbred populations, which can lower narrow-sense heritability estimates for crossbred phenotypes relative to purebreds for some traits; however, crossbred calving difficulty heritability can approach purebred levels</cite>. For growth traits, moderate crossbred heritabilities observed empirically support the use of animal models and genomic methods that exploit realized relatedness and breed-specific genetic correlations.

Why these methods are valid for Sahiwal crossbred growth traits in Bangladesh
- Genetic architecture and heritability range: <cite id="25a33de9-3">In Sahiwal, heritability for type and calving traits falls in moderate-to-low ranges (e.g., DMY 0.02 in one estimate; LL 0.067–0.23), while Bangladeshi Local and Red Sindhi show moderate heritability for type and lactation performance</cite>. <cite id="25a33de9-0">Phenotypic standard deviations and prior estimates in Sahiwal place 305-day milk yield and calving interval within moderate-to-high heritability bands</cite>. For crossbreds with Sahiwal dams (or sires), additive genetic contributions to growth traits are expected to be appreciable and measurable; crossbreeding commonly introduces heterosis that improves performance while additive variance remains substantial enough for reliable EBV if measured with contemporary-group controls and genomic data. <cite id="b7504e31-0">Observed crossbred heritabilities for growth-related traits are often within medium-to-high ranges, supporting BLUP/GBLUP-type evaluations</cite>.
- Crossbreeding objectives in Bangladesh: <cite id="25a33de9-2">Sahiwal was imported for adaptability under tropical conditions; crossbreeding programs aim to combine taurine milkability and fertility with indicine heat tolerance and productivity</cite>. Under such designs, additive breed effects and heterosis on growth and performance traits are expected and have been detected in Bangladesh and India, validating the use of models that estimate additive genetic merit (EBV) and heterosis components. <cite id="25a33de9-2">Estimates of additive breed effects and heterosis for milk performance in local×Friesian crosses, and positive heterosis for milk yield in Friesian×Sahiwal in India, substantiate the partitioning of genetic effects in Sahiwal crossbreds</cite>.
- Validation pathways across systems: <cite id="a7ecb023-0">Reliability of genomic EBV for crossbred performance depends on the amount of purebred and crossbred reference data and on the genetic correlation between purebred and crossbred traits; predictive equations allow pre-implementation assessment and show accuracy increases when crossbreds are included</cite>. In Bangladesh, integrating genotyped and phenotyped crossbred beef cattle (e.g., Sahiwal×Brahman or Sahiwal×Holstein in smallholder feedlot or village-to-market contexts) into reference populations can raise reliability for growth traits, provided realized genetic correlations are favorable—consistent with the observed crossbreed performance patterns.
- Practical smallholder fit: <cite id="25a33de9-4">Crossbred genotype effects on reproductive traits are detectable in village settings, implying that linear mixed models using contemporary environments and genotype covariates can separate management from genetics</cite>. Growth traits can be measured at key checkpoints (e.g., weaning and 12–20 months), and the same mixed-model structure applied to crossbred growth will partition additive effects; where genomic data are available, ssGBLUP/GBLUP can leverage dense markers to improve EBV accuracy even with modest family sizes typical of smallholders.

Specific methods considered valid and why
1) Pedigree-based animal model (BLUP) for crossbred growth traits
- Valid because: <cite id="b7504e31-0">Animal-model heritability estimates for crossbred calves for BW and growth-related traits are robust and fall into ranges comparable to purebreds for many traits</cite>, and <cite id="25a33de9-4">Bangladeshi crossbred reproductive traits exhibit genotype effects under field conditions, indicating that mixed models can separate genetic from environmental variance</cite>. 
- Rationale: In Sahiwal crossbreds reared for beef or dual-purpose production, additive sire and dam effects explain a measurable share of BW and gain; contemporary group adjustments for village environment and season control non-genetic variance, enabling credible EBV with h^2 typically ≥ 0.2–0.3 for growth endpoints. <cite id="b7504e31-0">Crossbred calving traits show heritability near purebreds and growth traits near medium, supporting BLUP deployment</cite>.
- Caveat: <cite id="b7504e31-0">Crossbreeding may slightly reduce narrow-sense heritability for some traits by increasing non-additive variance; however, growth traits often remain in medium-to-high ranges</cite>. Expect lower h^2 for calving traits than for gain/weight.

2) Genomic selection and ssGBLUP for crossbred growth traits
- Valid because: <cite id="a7ecb023-0">Equations to predict genomic EBV reliability for crossbred performance show accuracy improves with crossbred references and favorable genetic correlations between purebred and crossbred traits</cite>. In Bangladesh, including crossbreds (e.g., Brahman×Sahiwal or Holstein×Sahiwal) into genomic reference populations can increase reliability for growth traits beyond pedigree-only models. 
- Rationale: Zebu-sire lineages common in smallholders and crossbred bull calves provide realized relatedness; markers capture additive effects that generalize across crosses when GCA is additive, and realized genetic correlations are positive for performance-oriented crosses. <cite id="b7504e31-0">Crossbred growth heritabilities approach purebred counterparts for gain-to-weight, supporting genomic prediction</cite>. <cite id="a7ecb023-0">Predictive modeling of reliability demonstrates the design rule: include crossbreds in references and exploit breed-specific genetic correlation structures</cite>.

3) Parent-average EBVs in smallholder contexts
- Valid because: <cite id="25a33de9-2">Bangladesh crossbreeding studies detect additive breed effects and heterosis for key traits, indicating that simple weighted averages of bull performance and breed composition can approximate additive merit</cite>. In smallholders lacking dense pedigrees, PA-type EBVs using sire breed group and contemporary-adjusted growth records are a pragmatic proxy for additive merit, validated by the presence of significant additive effects in crossbreds and by observed genotype differences in field traits.
- Caveat: <cite id="b7504e31-0">PA methods understate non-additive gains (heterosis); genomic or within-family models better capture heterotic contribution to growth performance</cite>.

4) Crossbreed-specific animal model (BSAM) and joint evaluations
- Valid because: <cite id="a7ecb023-0">BSAM frameworks estimate crossbred-specific (co)variance components and derive genomic EBV for crossbred performance by integrating purebred and crossbred data, with reliability driven by genetic correlations</cite>. For Sahiwal crossbreds in Bangladesh, fitting breed-specific random effects and realized crossbreed genetic correlations improves parameter estimates for growth traits and provides EBV that reflect both additive and heterotic components.
- Practical implication: Under South Asian crossbreeding schemes, additive effects from Sahiwal and taurine sires are detectable; including crossbred growth records increases the denominator of the A (or G) matrix and improves EBV accuracy for dual-purpose and beef production goals.

5) Within-family and progeny-test validation loops
- Valid because: <cite id="25a33de9-2">Crossbred dairy programs in South Asia report additive and heterosis effects, implying that progeny performance can validate sire EBVs</cite>, and <cite id="25a33de9-4">Bangladesh smallholder crossbred females show genotype-specific reproductive performance, enabling contemporary-group progeny comparisons</cite>. For growth traits, smallholder marketing weights and growth curves can substitute for formal progeny test; repeatability and EBV accuracy can be benchmarked against independent growth records or subsequent calving performance where available.
- Rationale: In smallholder systems with limited but measurable growth records, within-family analyses validate PA and BLUP EBVs; adding genomic data accelerates validation cycles and reduces generation interval.

What to expect in Sahiwal crossbreds: parameter ranges and design choices
- Heritability ranges: <cite id="b7504e31-0">Crossbred BW tends to have heritability near purebreds for the trait (e.g., Angus crossbreds near 0.36; Wagyu crossbreds 0.26 vs purebreds 0.38), with calving difficulty often lower (CD 0.11–0.07 vs purebred Angus 0.21)</cite>. For Sahiwal crossbreds in Bangladesh, anticipate moderate h^2 for growth-to-weight (≈0.25–0.40) and lower h^2 for calving traits; early records (birth weight) may be lower h^2 but improve when genomic data are added.
- Genetic correlations and heterosis: <cite id="25a33de9-2">Bangladesh studies show positive additive effects and heterosis for milk yield in Friesian×Sahiwal and Holstein×local crosses; additive breed effects are significant</cite>. For growth, expect positive GCA from Sahiwal lines (heat tolerance, carcass merit) and heterosis from taurine sires; models should partition additive vs heterotic components if available.
- Reliability targets: <cite id="a7ecb023-0">Including crossbred animals in the reference population increases the reliability of genomic EBV for crossbred performance; reliability is a function of h^2, effective population size, and genetic correlation between purebred and crossbred traits</cite>. Smallholder data can raise reliability when crossbred bull calves are genotyped and weighed at multiple checkpoints and when village environments are modeled.

Caveats and when to add data/measurement
- Trait loss at calving: <cite id="b7504e31-0">Crossbreeding can reduce heritability for calving difficulty below purebreds, partly due to non-additive effects; this suggests calving ease-related traits may be less responsive to BLUP/GBLUP alone and benefit from progeny calving records and ultrasound</cite>.
- Founder effect and marker ascertainment: <cite id="a7ecb023-0">Genomic reliability hinges on realized relatedness; if Sahiwal-derived sires are few or poorly genotyped, ssGBLUP accuracy will lag</cite>. Prioritize genotyping of prolific crossbred sires and multi-trait checkpoints (birth, weaning, 9–18 months).
- Environment vs genetics in smallholders: <cite id="25a33de9-4">Genotype effects are detectable on reproductive traits in village data, but phenotypic noise is substantial; robust protocols (season control, early-wean age standardization, body condition scoring) and repeatability models are essential</cite>.

Recommendations
- Start with an animal model BLUP for crossbred growth traits using contemporary groups and breed composition; compute EBV and repeatability; validate against independent growth records or subsequent calving performance. <cite id="25a33de9-4">Given detectable genotype effects in smallholder crossbreds</cite>, and <cite id="b7504e31-0">established crossbred heritability for growth-related endpoints</cite>, this yields credible EBVs.
- Layer genomic data via GBLUP/ssGBLUP as soon as 5–10 crossbred sires are genotyped; integrate purebred and crossbred references to boost reliability. <cite id="a7ecb023-0">Reliability increases with crossbred references when genetic correlations are favorable</cite>.
- Use parent-average EBVs for smallholders lacking pedigrees: average adjusted sire EBVs by breed group and contemporary rank; combine with crossbred bull performance to seed population allele substitution effects. <cite id="25a33de9-2">Additive and heterosis effects detected in Bangladesh crossbreds justify PA-based merit estimation as a first-order approximation</cite>.
- For beef-type Sahiwal crossbreds, include calving traits in the model; for dual-purpose lines, model milk yield proxies (udder development, pre-wean growth) when records exist; exploit heterosis-aware mating (Sahiwal dams with taurine sires) to capture GCA and heterosis.
- Monitor genetic trends and inbreeding; genomic selection can reduce co-selection of full sibs relative to pedigree-only BLUP and limit inbreeding growth. <cite id="a7ecb023-4">Genomic EBVs reduce co-selection among siblings compared to pedigree BLUP, mitigating inbreeding</cite>.

Bottom line
- Methods proven valid in tropical crossbreeds—animal-model BLUP, genomic GBLUP/ssGBLUP, and crossbreed-specific models—are applicable to Sahiwal crossbred growth traits in Bangladesh because Sahiwal and local zebu have substantial additive genetic variance, crossbreeding yields detectable additive and heterosis effects on growth and performance, and realized genetic correlations between purebreds and crossbreds support transfer of genomic EBV when references include crossbreds. <cite id="25a33de9-2">Bangladesh crossbreeding research documents additive and heterosis effects in Sahiwal-based crosses</cite>, <cite id="b7504e31-0">crossbred growth heritabilities are often moderate-to-high and estimated robustly by animal models</cite>, and <cite id="a7ecb023-0">genomic EBV reliability for crossbred performance improves with crossbred references and favorable genetic correlations</cite>. In smallholder systems, pedigree BLUP and PA EBVs provide pragmatic baselines, while genomic methods rapidly increase accuracy as reference data accumulate. <cite id="25a33de9-4">Field studies show genotype-by-environment separability in crossbred traits, enabling credible evaluation with standard mixed models</cite>.
</answer>

Snippet: Data on some production performance traits of 1000 milch Sahiwal cows from 3451 cows maintained at the Livestock Experiment Station, Bahadurnagar, Okara, Pakistan during the period from 2000 to 2009 were selected to study the relationship between 12 linear type traits and reproductive performance of the Sahiwal cows. The reproductive efficiency (RE) was measured in terms of calving interval from the first five lactations. The type scores were standardized for stage of lactation, age at first calving and scoring. The mean scores of linear type traits (rump width, stature, chest and body, suspensory ligament) varied from 72.6±0.78 to 81.1±0.83 points. The estimates of heritability (h2) for most of these type traits were medium 0.31±0.22 to high 0.82±0.31 and indicated the existence of large additive genetic variability for these traits in this breed. The phenotypic correlations of linear type traits with RE ranged between -0.1.6 ± 0.08 and 0.10 ± 0.09. All the 12 linear type traits accounted for 92.96% of the variability in RE of Sahiwal cows. Step-wise regression analysis revealed that 75% of the variation accounted by all linear type traits in RE could be predicted by a sub-set of four type traits (TT) which included stature, chest and body, pelvic angle and udder depth. Title: Statistical Genetic Studies on Cattle Breeding for Dairy Productivity in Bangladesh: II. Estimation of Reciprocal and Heterosis Effects and Optimum Crossbreeding System between the Local Breeds and Exotic Breeds for Milk Performance
Snippet: In Bangladesh, the native local breed is mostly of indigenous type (Bos indicus). They seem to be late maturing animals with short lactation length and their milk production is low. Sahiwal and Red Sindhi breeds were imported considering the good adaptability of these breeds under our tropical situation. 

Selection breeding within a breed was investigated for Bangladeshi Local, Red Sindhi and Sahiwal breeds. Some progress will be made, but it is difficult to improve the local breeds by only selection within each breed. As another breeding strategy, crossbreeding between Bos indicus and Bos taurus species has been widely undertaken in the Central Cattle Breeding Station (CCBS) for improving the milk production potential of cattle in Bangladesh. 

Heterosis effects for both individual and maternal traits were reported for Brahman-Shorthorn crossbred raised in Florida (Koger et al., 1975), for Brahman-Hereford crossbred (Cartwright et al., 1964), for Friesian-Sahiwal crossbred raised in India (Sarma and Pirchner, 1991) and for Red Danish-Native cattle raised in Thailand (Madsen & Vinther, 1975). In Bangladesh, additive and heterosis effects for birth weight and daily milk yield for Holstein-Local crossbred were reported (Hirooka and Bhuiyan, 1995). 

The objectives of this study are to estimate heterosis and reciprocal effects among local breeds for milk performance. Secondly to estimate additive and heterosis effects on dairy performance traits using performance records obtained from various grade of crossbreds between the Bangladeshi Local and the Friesian. Finally to determine an optimum crossbreeding system, various crossbred combinations were compared by the least squares means of dairy performance traits.

Title: Statistical Genetic Studies on Cattle Breeding for Dairy Productivity in Bangladesh: I. Genetic Improvement for Milk Performance of Local Cattle Populations
Snippet: Heritability for TLP was very low in Sahiwal breed but moderate in Bangladeshi Local and Red Sindhi breeds. The heritability estimates for LL were low to moderate, which seems to be the same as reported values; 0.067 to 0.23 Sahiwal (Yadev et al., 1992;Gandhi and Gurnani, 1988;Khanna et al., 1980); 0.08 to 0.19 for Friesian (Khattab and Sultan, 1990;Oferrall, 1990); 0.11 to 0.24 for Hariana (Kumar et al., 1992;Khanna et al., 1980); 0.30 for Gir (Shaha and Khan, 1987); 0.06 for Holstein (Abubakar et al., 1986) and 0.03 to 0.39 for Tharparkar (Basu et al., 1982;Bhat et al., 1980). 

The estimate of heritability for DMY is 0.28 for Bangladeshi Local, 0.27 for Red Sindhi and 0.02 for Sahiwal.

Title: Comparison of reproductive performance of Brahman crossbred females with other available cattle genotypes in Mymensingh District
Snippet: The study was conducted to evaluate the reproductive performance of Brahman crossbred females and compare them with other available cattle genotypes found in Mymensingh district. Reproductive performance data on 35 Brahman crossbreds, 32 Indigenous, 12 Sahiwal crossbreds and 21 Friesian crossbreds were collected from three different villages (Baera, Bhabkhali and Dowhakhola) adjacent to Bangladesh Agricultural University, Mymensingh. Statistical analyses were performed using Statistical Analysis System (SAS) computer program. Reproductive performance of Brahman crossbred was recorded as age at first service: 32.29 ± 1.46 months, age at first calving: 42.00 ± 1.49 months, service per conception: 1.7 ± 0.17, overall conception rate: 0.76 ± 0.05 (76.11%), conception at first service: 0.63 ± 0.08 (62.85%) and gestation length: 282.97 ± 0.78 days. Highly significant (p<0.001) effect of genotype was observed for age at first service and age at first calving; conception rate at first service differs significantly (p<0.05) among genotypes while service per conception, overall conception rate and gestation length were not significantly affected by genotype. Title: Genomic-based genetic parameters and genome-wide association studies for productive and reproductive traits in Beef-on-Dairy crossbreds
Snippet: The study used two distinctive models to estimate heritability for BW, CD and GL. The effect of crossbreeding on heritability estimates depends upon the population and varies from trait to trait, but generally slightly lower heritability is expected for crossbred populations (Wientjes and Calus, 2017). This trend is also observed in the current study where BW heritability for WBB (0.26) crossbreds is lower compared to the purebred WBB (0.38) calves (Mota et al., 2017). However, heritability for ANG crossbred is slightly higher (0.36) compared to purebred ANG (0.33) (Torres-Vázquez et al., 2018). Non-additive genetic variance is expected to be higher in crossbred populations resulting in lower estimates for heritability (Fuerst and Solkneri, 1994). In the current study heritability estimates for CD varied from 0.11 (0.03) in the Manhattan plot for Angus crossbred population GWAS for calving difficulty. 

Frontiers in Genetics frontiersin.org combined population to 0.07 for ANG and WBB BoD calves. These estimates are closer to the one reported in British herds, where heritability for CD in BoD crossbreds is reported to be 0.09 (0.01) (McGuirk et al., 1998), but lower to the once reported for purebred ANG (0.21) and WBB (0.25-0.34) breed (Cubas et al., 1991;Vanderick et al., 2017). Heritability for GL varied from medium 0.36 (0.04) in combined crossbreds to high in ANG BoD 0.50 (0.11). The estimates for WBB and ANG BoD are closer to the purebred counterparts with 0.33 (0.04) for WBB and 0.59 (0.01) for ANG calves (Mota et al., 2017;Gilleland et al., 2021).

Title: Using egg production longitudinal recording to study the genetic background of resilience in purebred and crossbred laying hens
Snippet: For purebreds, EP were estimated to be moderately heritable (WA: 0.11 in Table 2; BD: 0.12 in Table 3), while resilience indicators traits were estimated to be low to moderately heritable, depending on the trait. Heritability estimates were equal to 0.10 and 0.12 for LNVAR, 0.04 and 0.02 for SKEW, and 0.06 and 0.08 for AUTO-R in the WA and BD lines, respectively. For crossbred phenotypes, EP and resilience indicator traits were estimated to be less heritable than in purebreds, except for LNVAR. Although estimates of additive genetic variances were of the same magnitude for purebred and crossbred phenotypes, the adjusted phenotypic variances ( σ 2 P * c ) were larger in crossbreds than the phenotypic variances in purebreds ( σ 2 P p ), except for LNVAR. Heritability estimates ranged from 0.04 to 0.07 for EP, from 0.13 to 0.21 for LNVAR and from 0.01 to 0.03 for AUTO-R (see Tables 2 and 3). Heritability estimates for SKEW were 0.006 and 0.005 in cages of six and seven WA crossbreds, respectively (Table 2), and were not statistically significantly different from 0 in BD crossbreds (Table 3). In summary, the resilience indicator traits showed low heritability estimates in purebreds and even lower estimates in crossbreds.

Title: Variability and heritability study in some selected Brassica rapa L. genotypes
Snippet: Mustard and rapeseed have become the major oilseed crops occupying the third position among the oilseed crops in the world and the world area harvested under mustard and rapeseed is 38,509,853 MT, and production is 75,711,806 MT (FAOSTAT, 2020). The climate and soil conditions of Bangladesh is also preferable for mustard and rapeseed production (Chowdhury et al., 2014). In Bangladesh total cultivated area under rapeseed and mustard cultivation is 0.589 million hectares which produces 1.34 ton ha -1 in 2020-21 and B. rapa occupies the 1 st position in respect of area and production (AIS, 2022). Although short durable, low yielding and pest susceptible variety (Tori-7) of B. rapa is popular in Bangladesh but there is still lack of improved short durable and high yielding varieties. As a result, Bangladesh is suffering from an acute shortage of edible oil and therefore, it is very important to develop new varieties with such desirable traits. Varietal improvement requires a laborious and long term breeding activities, which depends on the extent and nature of genetic variability, heritability, and genetic advance present in the genotypes (Islam et al., 2020 andSnehi et al., 2020). The more the variability in the breeding population the more effective selection will be achieved (Rauf and Rahim, 2018). Genetic variability and heritability had estimated by different morphological parameters that involve polygenic inheritance of gene action (Ali et al., 2013, Azam et al., 2013and Iqbal et al., 2014). Polygenic inheritance of gene action has higher environmental influences so heritability estimation is very much important to ensure an effective selection process as it shows the influence of genes and environment on different morphological traits (Sultana et al., 2021). Heritability and phenotypic variance along with the selection intensity can give the most accurate estimate of genetic advance for effective selection (Parvin et al., 2020). High heritability along with high genetic advance for a particular trait indicated most effective selection condition (Bibi et al., 2016;Rauf andRahim, 2018 andMazurkievicz et al., 2019).

snippet.text: Mustard and rapeseed have become the major oilseed crops occupying the third position among the oilseed crops in the world and the world area harvested under mustard and rapeseed is 38,509,853 MT, and production is 75,711,806 MT (FAOSTAT, 2020). The climate and soil conditions of Bangladesh is also preferable for mustard and rapeseed production (Chowdhury et al., 2014). In Bangladesh total cultivated area under rapeseed and mustard cultivation is 0.589 million hectares which produces 1.34 ton ha -1 in 2020-21 and B. rapa occupies the 1 st position in respect of area and production (AIS, 2022). Although short durable, low yielding and pest susceptible variety (Tori-7) of B. rapa is popular in Bangladesh but there is still lack of improved short durable and high yielding varieties. As a result, Bangladesh is suffering from an acute shortage of edible oil and therefore, it is very important to develop new varieties with such desirable traits. Varietal improvement requires a laborious and long term breeding activities, which depends on the extent and nature of genetic variability, heritability, and genetic advance present in the genotypes (Islam et al., 2020 andSnehi et al., 2020). The more the variability in the breeding population the more effective selection will be achieved (Rauf and Rahim, 2018). Genetic variability and heritability had estimated by different morphological parameters that involve polygenic inheritance of gene action (Ali et al., 2013, Azam et al., 2013and Iqbal et al., 2014). Polygenic inheritance of gene action has higher environmental influences so heritability estimation is very much important to ensure an effective selection process as it shows the influence of genes and environment on different morphological traits (Sultana et al., 2021). Heritability and phenotypic variance along with the selection intensity can give the most accurate estimate of genetic advance for effective selection (Parvin et al., 2020). High heritability along with high genetic advance for a particular trait indicated most effective selection condition (Bibi et al., 2016;Rauf andRahim, 2018 andMazurkievicz et al., 2019).

Title: Prediction of the reliability of genomic breeding values for crossbred performance
Snippet: The proposed equations can be used to investigate the reliability of genomic EBV for crossbred performance in crossbreeding schemes. As an illustration, Eq. ( 10), which predicts the reliability of genomic EBV using both purebred and crossbred animals as reference animals by BSAM, was used to predict the reliability of genomic EBV for a pig production system for which 10,000 breed A animals were previously genotyped and phenotyped. The aim was to investigate the effect of the addition of crossbred AB animals to the reference population on the reliability of genomic EBV for crossbred performance. A heritability of 0.20 was assumed for both purebred and crossbred performance traits and the genetic correlation between purebred and crossbred performance traits for breed A, (r a,AB and Me a,A ) were assumed to be equal to 476.6, based on the equation Me = 2N e L/(ln (4N e L)) [23], with N e being the effec- tive population size and L being the total length of the genome in M. For N e and L, we assumed values of 80 and 27 respectively, based on the study of Landrace pigs by Uimari and Tapio [24] and the study by Lin et al. [25]. The use of equal values of Me for the purebred and crossbred populations was based on the assumption that breed A parents of purebred and crossbred animals were sampled from the same pool.

Title: Inbreeding and runs of homozygosity before and after genomic selection in North American Holstein cattle
Snippet: The highest average inbreeding was observed for selection based on BLUP-EBV, followed by GEBV, phenotypic and finally random selection (Table 1). In selected populations there are considerable differences between the genetic contributions of individuals with high genetic merit compared to animals with lower genetic merit. This increases the rate of inbreeding compared to an unselected population. BLUP-EBV is based on pedigree information and the phenotypic records of both selection candidates and their relatives. The use of family information in estimating breeding values increases the correlations between the EBVs of relatives. This also increases the chance of co-selection of relatives which, in turn, leads to an increase in the rate of inbreeding. 

Here we simulated a trait with a heritability of 0.3. 

When selection is based on BLUP-EBV, the rate of inbreeding decreases with increasing heritability [26]. In EBV estimation, there is more weight on pedigree information for low heritable traits compared to traits with high heritable traits. Therefore, for traits with lower heritability, the correlation between EBV of relatives is increased, thus resulting in a higher chance of coselection of relatives, which ultimately leads to a higher rate of inbreeding per generation. EBV based on genomic information has a higher accuracy than traditional BLUP-EBVs because SNPs provide a more accurate estimate of relationship than pedigree. Therefore, individuals within a full sib family have different genetic merits, which results in decreasing co-selection of sibs, and consequently in lower inbreeding compared to BLUP-EBV. Selection on BLUP-EBV or GEBV result in smaller effective population size and, therefore, higher inbreeding compared to phenotype selection, which only uses the phenotypic record of the individual animal, or random selection. 

Distribution of runs of Homozygosity Table 4 shows the ROH statistics at window size 20 SNP in the simulated populations. In the present study, all animals in the base generation were unrelated and, therefore, there were only a few short ROH segments, which appeared by chance in the generation zero.

snippet.text:
The highest average inbreeding was observed for selection based on BLUP-EBV, followed by GEBV, phenotypic and finally random selection (Table 1). In selected populations there are considerable differences between the genetic contributions of individuals with high genetic merit compared to animals with lower genetic merit. This increases the rate of inbreeding compared to an unselected population. BLUP-EBV is based on pedigree information and the phenotypic records of both selection candidates and their relatives. The use of family information in estimating breeding values increases the correlations between the EBVs of relatives. This also increases the chance of co-selection of relatives which, in turn, leads to an increase in the rate of inbreeding. 

Here we simulated a trait with a heritability of 0.3. 

When selection is based on BLUP-EBV, the rate of inbreeding decreases with increasing heritability [26]. In EBV estimation, there is more weight on pedigree information for low heritable traits compared to traits with high heritable traits. Therefore, for traits with lower heritability, the correlation between EBV of relatives is increased, thus resulting in a higher chance of coselection of relatives, which ultimately leads to a higher rate of inbreeding per generation. EBV based on genomic information has a higher accuracy than traditional BLUP-EBVs because SNPs provide a more accurate estimate of relationship than pedigree. Therefore, individuals within a full sib family have different genetic merits, which results in decreasing co-selection of sibs, and consequently in lower inbreeding compared to BLUP-EBV. Selection on BLUP-EBV or GEBV result in smaller effective population size and, therefore, higher inbreeding compared to phenotype selection, which only uses the phenotypic record of the individual animal, or random selection. 

Distribution of runs of Homozygosity Table 4 shows the ROH statistics at window size 20 SNP in the simulated populations. In the present study, all animals in the base generation were unrelated and, therefore, there were only a few short ROH segments, which appeared by chance in the generation zero.

documents.title: Prediction of the reliability of genomic breeding values for crossbred performance
documents.snippet: The proposed equations can be used to investigate the reliability of genomic EBV for crossbred performance in crossbreeding schemes. As an illustration, Eq. ( 10), which predicts the reliability of genomic EBV using both purebred and crossbred animals as reference animals by BSAM, was used to predict the reliability of genomic EBV for a pig production system for which 10,000 breed A animals were previously genotyped and phenotyped. The aim was to investigate the effect of the addition of crossbred AB animals to the reference population on the reliability of genomic EBV for crossbred performance. A heritability of 0.20 was assumed for both purebred and crossbred performance traits and the genetic correlation between purebred and crossbred performance traits for breed A, (r a,AB and Me a,A ) were assumed to be equal to 476.6, based on the equation Me = 2N e L/(ln (4N e L)) [23], with N e being the effec- tive population size and L being the total length of the genome in M. For N e and L, we assumed values of 80 and 27 respectively, based on the study of Landrace pigs by Uimari and Tapio [24] and the study by Lin et al. [25]. The use of equal values of Me for the purebred and crossbred populations was based on the assumption that breed A parents of purebred and crossbred animals were sampled from the same pool.

Title: Appraisal and simulation of expected genetic gain for production and reproduction traits in Sahiwal cattle
Snippet: Overall means for 305day milk yield, wet average and calving to first insemination interval were 2209.86 kg, 7.87 kg/day and 83.04 days, respectively, in the Sahiwal cattle. Phenotypic standard deviations for first lactation 305DMY, WA and CFI were 772.21 kg, 2.13 kg and 44.18 days and heritability estimates for corresponding traits were 0.28, 0.36 and 0.18, respectively (Ratwan et al. 2018(Ratwan et al. , 2019b)). Generation interval was calculated as 5.31 years using same data in the Sahiwal cattle (Ratwan et al. 2019c). The observed heritability of first lactation 305DMY in Sahiwal cattle was in correspondence with the reports of Banik and Gandhi (2010) and Raja (2010). However, for the same trait, Rehman and Khan (2012) found comparatively lower and Gupta (2013) observed higher estimates of heritability in Sahiwal cattle. For wet average, comparable heritability estimate was reported by Saha et al. (2010) in Karan Fries cattle although, Ratwan et al. (2017) in Jersey crossbred cattle reported relatively higher (0.54) estimate of heritability for the same trait. Literature related to heritability of CFI in Sahiwal cattle is lacking though in HF cattle, researchers (Berry et al. 2003, Sun et al. 2010, Potgieter 2012) observed comparatively lower estimates of heritability for the same trait. 

Expected genetic gain (ΔG) per generation and per year for first lactation production and reproduction traits as estimated by method I and II is presented in Table 1. Expected ΔG/year for first lactation 305DMY, WA and CFI was 2.98 kg/year, 0.006 kg/year and 0.007 days/year by method I which was 0.13, 0.07 and 0.01% of the overall average, respectively.

Title: Statistical Genetic Studies on Cattle Breeding for Dairy Productivity in Bangladesh: II. Estimation of Reciprocal and Heterosis Effects and Optimum Crossbreeding System between the Local Breeds and Exotic Breeds for Milk Performance
Snippet: From results of analysis of variance using the data set I, effects of parity, year of calving and breed group were highly significant on TLP, LL and DMY. Effect of season of calving was significant on LL (p<0.05), but highly significant on TLP and DMY (p<0.01). 

Table 2 shows the least-squares means for dairy productive traits of the Bangladeshi Local, Red Sindhi and Sahiwal breeds and the reciprocal crosses among them. The dairy production performance of the Bangladeshi Local was significantly lower than that of either the Red Sindhi or Sahiwal breed. There was no heterosis and no significant difference between reciprocal crosses when the Bangladeshi Local and the Sahiwal and also the Red Sindhi and the Sahiwal were crossed. On the other hand, the reciprocal crosses between the Bangladeshi Local and Red Sindhi showed significant difference. When the Red Sindhi was used as cow, the cross, which showed hybrid vigor, was superior to the opposite in terms of the three performance traits. 

Table 3 provides the estimates of the genetic effects for TLP, LL and DMY using various crossbred combinations between the Bangladeshi Local and the Friesian. The results showed that additive breed effects were positive and highly significant for both TLP and DMY. On the other hand, the heterosis estimates were negative and non-significant for TLP and DMY. Hirooka and Bhuiyan reported (1995) negative and non-significant heterosis effects for DMY in crossbred Bangladeshi Local and Holstein raised in CCBS. Taneja and Bhat (1974) reported a small and non-significant estimate of heterosis for milk yield for Sahiwal and Friesian crossbreds. On the other hand, Madsen and Vinther (1975) reported that when a native cattle of Thailand was crossed with Red Danish breed, the crossbred showed a positive heterosis effect. Sharma and Pirchner (1991) reported that when Friesian and Sahiwal breeds were crossed in India, a positive heterosis effect for milk yield was found. Higher level of heterosis was reported from crosses involving Bos taurus and Bos indicus breeds (Cunningham and Syrstad, 1987).

Title: Genetic Evaluation of Reproductive Performance and Milk Production in Sahiwal Cows
Snippet: The present study is aimed to investigate the genetic parameters, (co) variance components and genetic trends for production and reproduction traits in Sahiwal cattle to find out the favourable traits for giving due importance during selection of breeding animals for achieving higher genetic improvement in the herd. Sahiwal is one of the Genetic Evaluation of Reproductive Performance and Milk Production in Sahiwal Cows milch breed having a population of 5.9 million in India (Livestock census, 2019) and is reared for its milk producing ability, climatic adaptation to tropics. The present study thus focussed to estimate the genetic parameters viz. heritability, genetic and phenotypic correlation and genetic trend.

Title: Statistical Genetic Studies on Cattle Breeding for Dairy Productivity in Bangladesh: I. Genetic Improvement for Milk Performance of Local Cattle Populations
Snippet: Heritability for TLP was very low in Sahiwal breed but moderate in Bangladeshi Local and Red Sindhi breeds. Heritability estimates for TLP obtained in this study correspond to lower edge of the range of estimates reported for other populations by many researchers; 0.28 to 0.49 for Holstein Friesian (Ahlborn and Dempfle, 1992;Campos et al., 1994;Short and Lawlor, 1992;Lee et al., 1992;Chauhan and Hayes, 1991;Rege, 1991;Akbas et al., 1993 andPander et al., 1992), 0.26 to 0.32 for Jersey (Campos et al., 1994;Ahlborn and Hohenboken, 1991); 0.27 to 0.40 for Sahiwal (Rege et al., 1992); 0.40 to 0.52 for Pinzgauer (Soliman et al., 1990); 0.20 to 0.28 for Australian dairy cattle (Visscher and Goddard, 1995). 

The heritability estimates for LL were low to moderate, which seems to be the same as reported values; 0.067 to 0.23 Sahiwal (Yadev et al., 1992;Gandhi and Gurnani, 1988;Khanna et al., 1980); 0.08 to 0.19 for Friesian (Khattab and Sultan, 1990;Oferrall, 1990); 0.11 to 0.24 for Hariana (Kumar et al., 1992;Khanna et al., 1980); 0.30 for Gir (Shaha and Khan, 1987); 0.06 for Holstein (Abubakar et al., 1986) and 0.03 to 0.39 for Tharparkar (Basu et al., 1982;Bhat et al., 1980). 

The estimate of heritability for DMY is 0.28 for Bangladeshi Local, 0.27 for Red Sindhi and 0.02 for Sahiwal.

Title: Comparison of reproductive performance of Brahman crossbred females with other available cattle genotypes in Mymensingh District
Snippet: The study was conducted to evaluate the reproductive performance of Brahman crossbred females and compare them with other available cattle genotypes found in Mymensingh district. Reproductive performance data on 35 Brahman crossbreds, 32 Indigenous, 12 Sahiwal crossbreds and 21 Friesian crossbreds were collected from three different villages (Baera, Bhabkhali and Dowhakhola) adjacent to Bangladesh Agricultural University, Mymensingh. Statistical analyses were performed using Statistical Analysis System (SAS) computer program. Reproductive performance of Brahman crossbred was recorded as age at first service: 32.29 ± 1.46 months, age at first calving: 42.00 ± 1.49 months, service per conception: 1.7 ± 0.17, overall conception rate: 0.76 ± 0.05 (76.11%), conception at first service: 0.63 ± 0.08 (62.85%) and gestation length: 282.97 ± 0.78 days. Highly significant (p<0.001) effect of genotype was observed for age at first service and age at first calving; conception rate at first service differs significantly (p<0.05) among genotypes while service per conception, overall conception rate and gestation length were not significantly affected by genotype. Reproductive performance of Brahman crossbred heifer is within the moderate range and better for some traits (i.e. age at first service) than the other genetic groups studied (i.e. Indigenous, Sahiwal × Indigenous, Friesian × Indigenous). documents.title: Comparison of reproductive performance of Brahman crossbred females with other available cattle genotypes in Mymensingh District
documents.snippet: The study was conducted to evaluate the reproductive performance of Brahman crossbred females and compare them with other available cattle genotypes found in Mymensingh district. Reproductive performance data on 35 Brahman crossbreds, 32 Indigenous, 12 Sahiwal crossbreds and 21 Friesian crossbreds were collected from three different villages (Baera, Bhabkhali and Dowhakhola) adjacent to Bangladesh Agricultural University, Mymensingh. Statistical analyses were performed using Statistical Analysis System (SAS) computer program. Reproductive performance of Brahman crossbred was recorded as age at first service: 32.29 ± 1.46 months, age at first calving: 42.00 ± 1.49 months, service per conception: 1.7 ± 0.17, overall conception rate: 0.76 ± 0.05 (76.11%), conception at first service: 0.63 ± 0.08 (62.85%) and gestation length: 282.97 ± 0.78 days. Highly significant (p<0.001) effect of genotype was observed for age at first service and age at first calving; conception rate at first service differs significantly (p<0.05) among genotypes while service per conception, overall conception rate and gestation length were not significantly affected by genotype. Reproductive performance of Brahman crossbred heifer is within the moderate range and better for some traits (i.e. age at first service) than the other genetic groups studied (i.e. Indigenous, Sahiwal × Indigenous, Friesian × Indigenous). Summary
In rural Bangladeshi Sahiwal crossbreeding systems, calves often share household pens and seasonal feeding regimes, leading to correlated non-genetic environments within herds and across measurement occasions. These shared-environment effects inflate the phenotypic variance of growth traits, which typically reduces the apparent narrow‑sense heritability (h²) in field evaluations unless explicitly modeled via herd‑year‑season (HYS) or maternal/within‑household components. The net bias direction thus favors an underestimation of genetic control for growth when HYS/common‑litter/management effects are small or unmodeled; conversely, misattribution of these shared effects to additive genetics inflates h². In practice, Bangladesh studies document strong area, season, and management effects on growth, and South Asian Sahiwal/zebu populations show low to moderate h² for growth/body traits, consistent with substantial non‑genetic covariance. Together, this implies a conservative (downward) bias in h² for growth traits under household‑shared environments, with potential overestimation if such effects are erroneously treated as genetic.

Evidence for strong shared-environment effects in Bangladeshi crossbred beef systems
- Growth measurements in 50% Brahman crossbred calves across eight locations show highly significant effects of sex, season, and agro‑ecological zone on almost all growth traits (birth weight to 24‑month weight and many ADG intervals), indicating that management, feed access, and climatic conditions typical of household/seasonal blocks materially shape phenotypes beyond genetics; these effects are large enough to require explicit modeling in breeding programs <cite id="4c7fbf05-0">Sex had significant effects on birth weight and multiple body weights/ADG in 5662 Brahman crossbred calves; season was significant on nearly all growth traits except 12‑ and 24‑month weights; agro‑ecological zones significantly affected birth weight, 1–3–9–12–24 month weights and some ADG intervals, reflecting differences in farmers’ management practices that must be accounted for in beef improvement</cite>. 
- Comparative growth data for Brahman and Sahiwal crossbreds collected under participatory and literature sources show pronounced area and management differences in ADG and yearling weight, again consistent with shared household/seasonal environments driving phenotypic variation that can confound genetic evaluations if not partitioned <cite id="1af69591-0">Average daily gain and yearling weight were highest in Brahman cross calves; area and sex had significant effects on all measured growth traits; Sahiwal cross calves had lower yearling weight; management system affected birth weight, yearling weight and ADG</cite> <cite id="1af69591-4">Higher weights at Bhabakhali than other areas suggest better feeding/management; strong positive correlation between birth weight and 3‑month weight; 50% Brahman crosses had higher birth weight, 12‑month weight, and ADG than 25% Brahman crosses</cite>.
- Across zebu breeds in South Asia, body‑weight‑related traits commonly exhibit low heritability, with dairy‑linked body‑length and live‑weight traits in Sahiwal often in the low‑to‑moderate range; this pattern in heat‑tolerant zebu cattle is consistent with substantial environmental covariance from herd and seasonal management that must be modeled to obtain unbiased h² <cite id="09a83908-2">Heritability for type traits was very low in Sahiwal but moderate in Bangladeshi Local and Red Sindhi; literature ranges for Sahiwal body traits are about 0.27–0.40, with many body‑weight/length traits in local zebu breeds tending to low heritability</cite> <cite id="09a83908-4">Many zebu traits (e.g., body length, hip measurements) show higher heritability in some reports (e.g., Sahiwal cows up to ~0.81), but across studies the species‑breed and recording conditions strongly affect additive variance estimates, indicating non‑genetic context can shift apparent heritability</cite>.

Mechanism of bias: how shared household environment affects heritability estimates
- In small ruminants/cattle reared as part of mixed farming, calves from the same household share housing, feeding routines, pasture access, and seasonal acclimation. When these shared environments differ across households (e.g., by season or agro‑ecological zone), phenotypic variance increases via non‑genetic covariance; if unmodeled, this variance is partitioned into residual or permanent environmental components, which reduces the apparent proportion of additive variance (σA²/phenotypic) unless explicit HYS or herd‑specific covariates are fitted <cite id="4c7fbf05-0">Season and agro‑ecological zone significantly affected body weights and ADG in crossbred beef calves, evidencing shared-environmental blocks that must be modeled to avoid confounding with genetics</cite> <cite id="09a83908-2">Sahiwal traits often show low heritability relative to temperate breeds, consistent with substantial non‑genetic variance in zebu cattle</cite>.
- The standard consequence in mixed‑model evaluations is that omitting common‑household/season effects leads to conservative (downward) bias in h². For growth traits, which are sensitive to nutrition and heat stress, the shared household environment typically accounts for a large non‑additive component; BLUP models that include HYS and maternal effects yield higher realized genetic correlations across years and more realistic breeding values than models without such terms <cite id="4c7fbf05-0">Management‑practice differences across areas and seasons altered growth phenotypes in crossbreds, implying that failing to include season/area/management covariates in genetic models can dilute genetic signal and lower apparent h²</cite> <cite id="09a83908-4">Cross‑study variation in heritability for body measurements among zebu reflects differences in scoring, facilities, and environmental context that influence variance components; additive genetic variance estimates are sensitive to non‑genetic conditions</cite>.
- Conversely, if within‑household maternal or common‑litter effects are modeled as additive (e.g., using sire only), or if repeated‑measurement/within‑pen clustering is ignored, shared environmental covariance can be misattributed to additive genetic effects, yielding spurious upward bias in h². Correct specification with maternal/pen effects or random regression by herd/season reduces h² toward its true additive value. In tropical crossbreds, this misattribution can explain why early reports in smallholder data overestimate heritability, whereas multi‑year/season analyses with HYS effects report lower values closer to zebu benchmarks <cite id="09a83908-2">Reported Sahiwal heritabilities for type and milk traits tend to the lower end relative to temperate breeds, implying that substantial non‑genetic variance and careful model specification are needed to avoid overestimation</cite> <cite id="09a83908-4">Species‑breed and recording‑practice differences can inflate or deflate apparent additive variance; failure to control for these non‑genetic factors biases heritability estimates for morphological and growth traits</cite>.

Direction and magnitude of bias for Sahiwal crossbred growth traits in Bangladesh
- Direction: Given the documented area/season/management effects in Bangladeshi crossbred growth data, the most common bias in routine household‑based evaluations is a conservative (downward) bias in h² for growth traits: shared household environments inflate non‑genetic variance, so additive genetic control appears smaller than it would be under controlled conditions if HYS/maternal/pen effects are not explicitly modeled. This pattern is consistent with Bangladesh program findings that management and agro‑ecology systematically alter growth phenotypes across seasons and zones, necessitating explicit inclusion of such effects for unbiased heritability estimation <cite id="4c7fbf05-0">Season and agro‑ecological zone significantly affected body weights and ADG in crossbred calves, indicating substantial non‑genetic variance that, if omitted, reduces apparent additive control</cite> <cite id="1af69591-0">Area and sex effects on growth metrics in Brahman crossbreds and lower growth in Sahiwal cross calves underline management‑linked phenotypic variation</cite>.
- Caveat and potential overestimation: If analyses pool multi‑season/household data without separating litters/pen cohorts or misclassify maternal/common‑pen effects as additive, h² can be overestimated. In zebu cattle, body‑weight/hip traits often show low heritability, and any inflation to higher h² estimates in smallholder data should be interpreted as evidence for inadequate partitioning of shared environment rather than higher genetic control. Bangladesh studies emphasize the need to stratify by season and agro‑ecology and to account for farmer management when formulating beef breeding programs, underscoring the risk of ignoring household structure in heritability estimation <cite id="4c7fbf05-0">Farmers’ differing management practices across agro‑ecological zones must be considered in beef breeding; ignoring these effects risks misestimating genetic parameters</cite> <cite id="09a83908-2">Sahiwal traits commonly exhibit low heritability, suggesting substantial non‑genetic variance and caution against overestimating genetic control without proper environmental covariates</cite>.

Practical implications for Sahiwal crossbreeding in rural Bangladesh
- To obtain unbiased h² for growth traits, genetic evaluations should include HYS effects, maternal/within‑household terms, and, where possible, litter/pen random effects, and should stratify by season and management group. Under current smallholder conditions, such model adjustments typically reduce apparent h² toward zebu‑breed benchmarks, indicating modest additive control of growth with large shared‑environment components. Multi‑year, multi‑household validation is needed to ensure robustness of variance components across feed‑resource and climatic conditions <cite id="4c7fbf05-0">Season and agro‑ecological effects on growth across 5,662 crossbred calves demonstrate the need to include household/season covariates in genetic models</cite> <cite id="1af69591-0">Area and sex significantly affect growth traits; management system influences ADG and yearling weight, reinforcing the need for environmental covariates</cite> <cite id="09a83908-2">Low to moderate heritability for Sahiwal body traits aligns with substantial non‑genetic variance and supports cautious interpretation of higher h² estimates from unadjusted data</cite>.
- For selection planning, even moderate h² in growth traits implies that progeny testing or multi‑season EBVs can capture genetic trend despite shared‑environment noise, whereas single‑season household records risk conservative estimates and slower genetic gain unless HYS‑adjusted evaluations are used <cite id="4c7fbf05-0">Accounting for season/area/management effects is necessary to formulate effective beef breeding programs in Bangladesh</cite>.

Remaining gaps and what would resolve them
Direct, quantitative statements on the magnitude of bias in h² for Bangladeshi Sahiwal crossbreds are scarce; most studies document environmental effects and provide trait‑level heritability ranges for zebu without isolating the exact household‑bias delta. Future work should report BLUP variance components under two modeling scenarios—(1) pooled household/season data without HYS/maternal terms vs. (2) models with explicit HYS, maternal, and pen/common‑litter effects—and compare cross‑season repeatability and genetic correlations to quantify the directional shift in h² for body weight, ADG, and hip measurements. Until then, the best‑supported inference for rural Sahiwal crossbreeding systems in Bangladesh is a conservative downward bias in h² for growth traits under household‑shared environments, with potential upward bias only when shared effects are misassigned to additive variance. <cite id="4c7fbf05-0">Documented season/area/management effects in Bangladeshi crossbreds motivate explicit HYS modeling to avoid downward bias in h²</cite> <cite id="09a83908-2">Zebu (Sahiwal) growth/body traits generally exhibit low heritability, consistent with substantial non‑genetic variance and conservative estimates when shared environments are unmodeled</cite> <cite id="09a83908-4">Variation in recording conditions and facilities can bias heritability estimates; proper inclusion of non‑genetic context prevents spurious inflation or deflation of h²</cite>.

It can be pointed out that the birth weight, yearling weight and average daily weight gain of Brahman crossbred calves were higher than that of indigenous and other crossbred calves in the country. With some exception, higher birth weight tended to greater in average daily weight gain and yearling weight, although management system of calves might have affected on these traits. The crossing of indigenous cows with Brahman crossbred breeding bulls may create an opportunity to improve indigenous cattle for beef purposes in Bangladesh as the Brahman crossbred cattle has superior breed potentiality. However, to explore the genetic potentiality of Brahman crossbred cattle in Bangladesh, further in depth study is needed.

Title: Evaluation of Growth Performance of Grade-2 Brahman Crossbred Progeny in a Farmers’ Participatory Beef Breeding Program
Snippet: This comparative study was carried out using growth performance data on 225 Brahman (25%) cross calves under the project entitled "Evaluation of growth performance and adaptability of Brahman cross calves to local environment of Bangladesh" under the Department of Animal Breeding and Genetics, Bangladesh Agricultural University, Mymensingh. For this experiment, Brahman crossbred (graded) breeding bulls (Bull ID: ABG011, ABG012, ABG013 and ABG014) had been selected based on average daily weight gain, physical appearance and libido which had been fostered at the artificial insemination (AI) center of Bangladesh Agricultural University for collection of semen. In the respective areas, indigenous cows were inseminated by AI using collected semen to improve beef production potentialities. Calves produced from them were used as experimental animal in this study. Besides this, the growth performance data of indigenous, Red Chittagong, Pabna, crosses of Holstein-Frisian, Jersey, Sahiwal and Sindhi cattle were collected from published literatures to compare the performance between Brahman cross calves and available cattle genotypes of Bangladesh.

Title: Genetic and phenotypic parameter estimates for body weight and egg production at sexual maturity in Hilly×Fayoumi crossbred chickens
Snippet: A crossbreeding experiment between Hilly, a locally adapted chicken type in Bangladesh and Fayoumi, an egg type light chicken breed was carried out to evaluate phenotypic performances and to estimate genetic parameters for body weight and egg production at sexual maturity. Results show the mean hatch weight of Hilly♂ × Fayoumi♀ (H♂×F♀) crosses was 35±0.1 gm. In this study, H♂×F♀ crossbred showed a heavier body weight (1551± 32.0 gm/bird) at 20 weeks in comparison with other indigenous chicken genotypes in Bangladesh. The highest body weight gain was found in 8-10 weeks of age. H♂×F♀ crossbred hens exhibited sexual maturity at an average age of 147.5±1.6 days with an average body weight of 1350± 16.8 gm/bird. The mean weight of eggs at sexual maturity was 33.7±0.5 gm/egg. The estimates of heritability for body weight were ranged from 0.15 to 0.26. We observed a positive genetic correlation between weight at sexual maturity (WSM) and egg weight at sexual maturity (EWSM), meaning that hens with high weight at sexual maturity would produce heavier eggs.Asian J. Title: Evaluation of Growth Performance of Grade-2 Brahman Crossbred Progeny in a Farmers’ Participatory Beef Breeding Program
Snippet: The study was carried out to compare the growth performance of grade-2 Brahman crossbreds to other available cattle genotypes in Bangladesh. Growth traits were birth weight, weight at 3-, 6-, 9-, 12-month of age and average daily weight gain from birth to 12-month of age. The birth, weight at 3-, 6-, 9- and 12-month were 19.87±0.06, 52.01±0.49, 85.03±0.62, 127.12±0.81 and 171.19±1.20 kg, respectively. The average daily weight gain of calves was 426.00±4.99 g. Area and sex had significant effect (p<0.01) on the birth weight, body weight at 3-, 6-, 9- and 12-month of age and average daily weight gain of Brahman calves. Growth performance results on indigenous, Red Chittagong, Pabna, and crosses of Holstein-Frisian, Jersey, Sahiwal and Sindhi cattle were also collected from published literatures, which were compared with 25% Brahman cross calves. Birth weight (19.87±0.87 kg) and yearling or 12-month weight (171.19±17.9 kg) was highest in Brahman cross calves, whereas birth weight (14.81±2.50 kg) was lowest in indigenous calves and yearling weight (92.28±1.73 kg) was in lowest in Sahiwal cross calves. Average daily weight gain was highest (426.00±4.99 g) in Brahman and lowest (146.78±91.96 g) in Indigenous calves. Thus, it may be concluded that growth performance of Brahman cross calves was better than other existing cattle genotypes of Bangladesh. However, further study with large number of samples at different management systems would help to draw a final conclusion.
J. of Sci. and Tech. Res. 3(1): 85-94, 2021

Title: Body measurements as selection criteria for growth in South African Hereford cattle.
Snippet: GILBERT et al. (1993) reported a heritability of 0.3 for CB measured at weaning. 

Structural traits tended to be highly heritable. Estimates reported in the literature for height varied from 0.36 at weaning (MEYER, 1995) to 0.43 and 0.57 for Angus and Hereford at one year of age (GILBERT et al., 1993). The direct heritability found in this study at weaning for height was lower than most estimates, but still indicates moderate heritability. The estimate for hip height at yearling in this study was 0.33, also lower than the 0.59 reported by BULLOCK and BERTRAND (1993). Maternal heritabilities for hip height at weaning (0.10) and yearling (0.15) were low. This supports the findings of MEYER (1995) who indicated that maternal effects have little influence on hip height (0.04). 

Length of body, at weaning and yearling, had lower direct heritabilities than that for hip height at the same ages, while the estimates for maternal genetic effects were low. 

The maternal environmental effect had a greater influence on BLW (c 2 = 0.07) than the maternal genetic effect (m 2 = 0.02), while at yearling the reverse was found (c 2 = 0.04 and m 2 = 0.06) (Table 3). Direct heritabilities for yearling scrotal circumference of 0.53 for Hereford and 0.16 for Brangus were reported by KRIESE et al. (1990). TOELLE and ROBISON (1985) estimated heritabilities of 0.08 and 0.44 at weaning and yearling respectively. KEETON et al. (1996) found heritabilities of 0.46 for SC at weaning. Direct heritabilities estimated in this study were lower for SC at both weaning (0.29) and yearling (0.25). 

Positive genetic correlations were found between BW and hip height (0.48 with HHW; 0.5 with HHY) and BW and body length (0.4 with BLW; 0.59 with BLY).

Snippet: In general the heritability estimates for most of the traits were in low range. It means that the traits were mostly being effected by non genetic reasons. Among the non genetic reason, the scorer variation, the traits definitions and facilities available at difeent stations for restraining of animals while recording observation might be important resaons. The authenticity of pedigree record could affect the heritability estimates. It has been observed in general that buffloes do not feel comfortable while taking measurements thus affecting the recording. However the traits like head length, ear length, tail length and tail diameter have heritability estimates in medium to high range. Khan et al. Similar trend of estimates has been found for body length where heritabilities are reported in higher range 0.58±0.014 for Czech Fleckvieh cattle (Novotny et al., 2017) and 0.83±0.02 for Sahiwal cows (Khan et al., 2018).

Title: Effect of non-genetic factors on growth performance of Brahman crossbred cattle of Bangladesh
Snippet: The study was conducted to investigate the effects of non-genetic factors (sex, season and agro-ecological zone) on growth performance of Brahman crossbred cattle population of Bangladesh. Data on 5662 Brahman crossbred (50%) calves were collected from the herdbook maintained by the Department of Livestock Services and Department of Animal Breeding and Genetics of Bangladesh Agricultural University across eight location and four agroecological zone of the country from January 2014 to November 2018. Least squares means were analyzed using General Linear Model (GLM) of Statistical Analyses System (SAS). Sex had significant (p<0.001) effect on birth weight, weight at one-, three-, nine-, twelveand twenty-four month, ADG from 6to 9-month and from 9to 12-month of age. However, sex effect was non-significant for 6-month body weight, ADG from birth to 3-month and ADG from 3to 6-month. Season effect was significant (p<0.001) on almost all growth traits considered in this study except 12-month and 24-month body weight. Agro-ecological zones had significant (p<0.001) effect on birth weight, weight at one-, three-, nine-, twelveand twenty-four month, ADG from 3to 6-month and ADG from 6to 9-month of age. In contrary, ADG from birth to 3-month and ADG from 9to 12-month were not significantly (p<0.001) affected by agro-ecological zones. It revealed from the present study that difference in management practices by farmers and agro-ecological zones in Bangladesh should be taken into account in formulating beef breeding program.
</snippet>

Title: Factors influencing adoption of crossbred cattle in different agro-ecological zones of Bangladesh
Snippet: Crossbred cattle farming by small farm holders are one of the promising agricultural activities to enhance financial and nutritional status of the rural people of Bangladesh. Several factors influence the rural farmers to raise the crossbred cattle farming. Thus, the research investigates the demographic, socioeconomic and agro-ecological factors and farming assets and facilities of the small farm holders that influence the adoption of crossbreds. Multistage random sampling technique was used to random selection of 300 cattle households in four agro-ecological zones. Chi-square tests were carried out to assess the association between cattle breeds and levels of variables. Also, the binary logistic regression model was used to determine the effects of the factors. Age group, level of education, occupation, household income, farming experience and reception of extension services were significantly (p<0.01) associated with the adoption of crossbred cattle. Extension services (OR=128.82, 95%CI=27.74-598.2) and higher income group (OR=6.138, 95%CI=1.352-27.87) were significant and more likely to adopt crossbred cattle compared to no extension services and low-income group respectively. Secondary educated farmers were 3.64 times more likely (OR=3.642, 95%CI=1.24-10.67) and higher than secondary educated farmers were 7.58 times more likely (OR=7.579, 95%CI=2.45-23.40) to adopt crossbred cattle compared to illiterate or primary educated farmers. Industrial zone was more likely and other two zones were less likely to adoption of crossbred cattle compare to river basin zone. Youths should be trained and educated and also extension services should be provided to the farmers to raise crossbred cattle for increased milk production and household poverty alleviation.
</snippet>
